2. The relevant facts for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that Sam Miah, predecessor of respondent Nos. 1-10 instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif Sadar, Sylhet against the appellants and respondent Nos.11-33 for a declaration that the suit land described in schedule-II to the plaint belonged to the plaintiff in maliki right and the record of rights in respect of the suit land in the names of the predecessors of the defendants is wrong and incorrect and for recovery of khas possession of the suit land described in schedule-III to the plaint. The suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.28 of 1990 on transfer to the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Circuit Court, Sylhet. During pendency of the suit, Saru Miah died and his heirs, the present plaintiffs were substituted. 

 3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the land described in schedule-I of the plaint originally belonged to Mufti Zainuddin and others of Dargah Mahalla, Sylhet in maliki right. Sheikh Selim, father of Saru Miah, original plaintiff, was tenant [chakran] a service under the said landlords. While he [Sheikh Selim] was residing in one of the homesteads of the landlords at Longar Dewri with his family, he took a second wife and went to reside with the 2nd wife at Rajor Goli surrendering the possession of the said homestead in favour of landlords where he had been residing as service tenant. Sam Miah then took settlement of the land described in schedule-I to the plaint from the landlords and while residing there, took his mother with him, gave shelter to his other two brothers named Kantu Miah, predecessor of defendant No.1 and Charu Miah alias Abdul Khalique, predecessor of defendant Nos. 16-24 and also one Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-16 and another person named Jan Khan. Thereafter, the landlords instituted Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the 1st Court of Munsif Sadar, Sylhet for declaration of their title in the land of schedule-I of the plaint and recovery of khas possession against Sheikh Selim, Sara Miah and others who had been residing there and got a decree for declaration of title only. Against the said judgment and decree, Sam Miah filed Titie Appeal No.259 of 1953 before the District Judge, but subsequently, compromised the dispute and then by a registered kabala dated 22.09.1954 purchased the right, title and interest of the landlords in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and continued owning and possessing the same by his right of purchase. While possessing the same, plaintiff Saru Miah transferred 1 (one) powa land in favour of his brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique out of the land described in schedule-I by registered kabala and also transferred .005 decimal land out of the land described in schedule-I in favour of Tunu Miah, son of his other brother-Kantu. Miah by registered deed of gift dated 08.12.1979. During the field survey of the last survey and operation, settlement the lard described in schedule-1 was recorded in the names of the plaintiff and his brother according to their share, but recently by the first part of Baishakh, 1386 BS, the plaintiff came to know that the land in schedule-II had been wrongly recorded in the names of late Kantu Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11 and late Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14 beyond his knowledge. Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah were very close relatives of the plaintiff and they having no place to live in, sought for temporary shelter to the plaintiff and the plaintiff on compassionate ground allowed them to live in the land described in schedule-III on condition to move therefrom on arrangement of accommodation elsewhere. The plaintiff having learnt about the wrong record of rights of the land described in schedule-II in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah, demanded to defendant Nos.1-14 for correction of the record of rights and asked them to vacate the land described in schedule-III lastly by the last part of Baishakh, 1386 BS. Said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah had no right, title and interest whatsoever in the suit land. The wrong record of rights of the Land described in schedule-II to the plaint in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah has cast cloud over the title of the plaintiff. Hence, the plaintiff instituted the suit. 

 5. Defendant Nos.1 and 11 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the land described in schedule-I originally belonged to Mufti Zainuddin and others in maliki right and Sheikh Selim was the service tenant who used to reside in the scheduled land with his famkly and gave some portion of his land to Rashid Miah to reside therein. After sometime, Zaminders filed Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the Court of Munsif, Sylhet for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession by evicting Sheikh Selim and others. Sheikh Selim and his son-Chant Miah only contested the suit. In the said suit, the maliki right of the Zaminders was declared, but the prayer for recovery of possession was disallowed. After abolition of the Zamindari system by the operation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Sheikh Selim became a tenant under the Government in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and the rent receiving interests of the plaintiff which he purchased from the Zaminders was extinguished by operation of law. The plaintiff acquired no right to the possession of the suit land by his alleged purchase and that the plaintiff used to reside in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint with his father, Sheikh Selim. Thereafter, while possessing the land described in schedule-I, Sheikh Selim died leaving behind two sons named Kantu Miah and plaintiff-Saru Miah, one daughter Malika Bibi and four grandsons and three grand-daughters by his predeceased son, Sheikh Chart Miah @ Abdul Khalique and thus, by inheritance, the plaintiff acquired 1/7th share, Kantu Miah predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 and 11 got 2/7th share, the heirs of Chan: got 2/7th and daughter Malika got 1/7th share in the land described in schedule-1. Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14, was residing in a portion of the land described in schedule-1 to the plaint with the permission of Sheikh Selim and during the settlement operation, his name was recorded on the basis of possession though he has no title over the suit land. The record of rights in respect of Rashid Miah is not correct, it should have been recorded in the name of Sheikh Selim, Rashid Miah being a licensee the specific portion of land described in schedule-I under Sheikh Selim. The plaintiff Mliah sold .07 acre of land to Charu Abdul Khalique out of his share in the land described in schedule-I, he has subsisting interest in only to the plaint. 

 6. Defendant Nos. 2 (Ka) -2 (Ga) contended that the suit land is recorded in Plot No.4583. Sheikh Selim unlike his predecessor was possessing the suit land un Zaminder, Mufti Zainuddin and others and died leaving behind three sons named Kantu Miah, Saw Miah and Pharo Miah and 3[three] daughters named Monu Shofia Bibi and Alifan Bibi as his heirs who possessed the suit land and accordingly, the entire suit land was recorded in Plot No.4585 in their names. Thereafter, they handed over some portion of the land to Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14. Shofia Bibi died leaving behind two daughters named Ayesha Begum-defendant No. 2(Ka) and Champa and one son named Emani Miah as her heirs. Kantu Miah died leaving behind defendant Nos.1-11 as his heirs. Then Tunu Miah died leaving behind Ayesha Bibi, his wife, defendant No.2(Ka), one daughter named Reba Mom [ Minor-defendant No.2(Kha) and one son named Shailaz Miah defendant No.2(Gha) as his heirs who have been in possession of the suit plot. 

 7. Defendant Nos. 12-13 that Sheikh Selim and Rashid Miah had title and possession ill the suit land described in schedule-II to the plaint two equal shares and accordingly, the, share of Rashid Miah was rightly recorded in his name in the SA Khatian and While possessing the same, he died leaving behind defendant Nos.12-14 as his heirs and defendant Nos.12 and 13 have been possessing the same. For grabbing the land of these defendants, the plaintiff created false girding the Suit land documents regarding the Suit land. 

 8. Al the trial, the plaintiff examined 8[eight] witnesses including plaintiff No. 1[Ka] Rupon Miah as Pw-3 and the defendants examined 5[five] witnesses support of their respective eases. The learned Assistant Judge after framing 7[seven] issues, recording evidence, hearing the arguments of the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 31.07.1991 dismissed the suit. 

 9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 31.07.1991 passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.133 of 1991 before the learned Additional District and Sessions Judge, Sylhet who having heard the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 02.11.1997 dismissed the appeal affirming those of the trial Court. 

 10. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the Appellate Court, the plaintiff as petitioner filed Civil Revision No.486 of 1999 before the High Court Division. The learned Judge of the High Court Division having heard the respective parties and considering the materials on record by the judgment and order dated 21.08.2008 made the Rule absolute reversing those of the Courts below. 

 12. Mr. Mrinal Kanti Biswas, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellants, submits that the moot question in this case is whether Sheikh Selim, who was admittedly a service tenant in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint, under Zaminder, Mufti Zainuddin and others, had surrendered the possession of the aforesaid scheduled land in favour of the aforesaid landlords and thereafter, Saru Miah, original plaintiff, had taken settlement of the suit land described in schedule-I to the plaint from the said Zaminders or not. He further submits that the Court of Appeal below, the final Court of facts, on consideration of the evidence, particularly, exhibit-Ka[1], the certified copy of the plaint of Title Suit No.80 of 1951 and exhibit-Kha (1), the certified copy of the judgment of Title Suit No.80 of 1951, held that Sheikh Selim possessed the land described in schedule-I to the plaint as service tenant under the landlords and did not surrender possession thereof in favour of the landlords and that his son, Saru Miah, did not take settlement of the suit land from the Zaminder and the High therefore, Court Division committed serious error in holding that the Appellate Court below gave concurrent findings and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court simply by concurring with the findings of the trial Court without dis-cussing the evidence independently and thereby the High Court Division acted illegally in setting aside the decision of the Court of Appeal below, the final Court of facts and remanded the case to the Court of Appeal below for fresh decision occasioning miscarriage of justice. He further submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred to appreciate the concurrent findings of the Court below that Sheikh Selim, who was the service tenant, did not surrender possession of the suit land to his Zaminder, Mufti Zainuddin and others and Saru Miah had not taken settlement of the suit land from the Zaminders is being essentially a finding of facts based on oral as well as documentary evidence is immune from revision since the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not spell out any misreading or non-consideration of evidence done by the Court of Appeal below and in that view of the matter acted illegally in making the Rule absolute and sending the case back on remand for fresh decision based upon the evidence on record occasioning miscarriage of justice. 

 13. Mr. Md. Motahar Hossain, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-10, contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the High Court Division rightly found that the Courts below did not approach the case in proper perspective and both the Courts below were required to find that the plaintiffs had prayed for correction of the record of rights and eviction of some persons from the disputed land described in the said schedule who were claimed to be in permissive possession in the land described in schedule-III to the plaint and the Courts below ought to have decided the owner-ship of the plaintiffs in actual quantum of land. He further contends that the High Court Division, rightly held that the finding of the trial Court has no basis in fact or law since it is evident from the plaint and depositions that the plaintiffs did not pray for evicting anyone from the land described in schedule-II to the plaint an6 for recovery of khas possession. The plaintiffs rather sought for declaration of title along with correction of the record of rights regarding the land described in schedule-II to the plaint and recovery of khas possession of the land described in schedule-III to the plaint by evicting defendant No.1 therefrom. He further submits that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the Appellate Court below without discussing the evidence of PWs' and DWs' in light of their pleadings affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court below and allowed Cross Objection No.5 of 1992 and, therefore, non-consideration of the oral evidence of the parties in light of their respective cases vitiated the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Courts below. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as both the Courts below misconstrued the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record and their erroneous findings that the land described in schedule-II to the plaint is possessed by the defendants, and the plaintiffs cannot get the relief of recovery of khas possession without praying for recovery of khas possession of the entire Land described in schedule-II to the plaint are totally baseless and misconceived one and, moreover, the trial Court below also came to the erroneous conclusion that the suit is barred by limitation and that the suit is not duly stamped and, on a clear wrong approach to the cases of the parties, and their respective evidence led the Courts below to arrive at the erroneous conclusion with regard to the plaintiffs' possession over the suit land which has occasioned a serious miscarriage of justice. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as defendant Nos.1 and 11 filed a joint written statement, defendant Nos.2(Ka)-(Ga) filed another joint written statement, and defendant Nos.12 and 13 also filed another joint written statement denying the case of the plain-tiffs but the said defendants did not adduce any evidence in support of their written statements and, furthermore, the Appellate Court below without elaborate consideration of entire evidence, both oral and documentary, held that the plaintiffs have not proved their title in the land described in schedule-II to the plaint, and allowed the cross objection, although the trial Court below came to a clear finding that the plaintiffs have their title over the suit land but no possession was maintained by the plaintiffs and, thus, the Courts below committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiffs have proved their case. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as PW-2 stated in his deposition that he knows the plaintiff, Sam Miah, and his heirs and he also knows the father of plaintiff, Sam Miah, namely, Sheikha Selim, and he also stated that he knows Sheikh Selim since his childhood, and Pw-3, Rupon Miah, as substituted plaintiff deposed on behalf of the plaintiffs, and he supported the plaintiffs' case, and Pw-4 corroborated the plaintiffs' case. He further contends that Pws'- 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8 corroborated the case of the plaint, but both the trial Court below and the Appellate Court below without considering the evidence of all the Pws' and Dws' dismissed the suit and, thus, non-consideration of the said evidence by the Courts below caused a serious miscarriage of justice. It is further submitted that they High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the trial Court below did not at all discuss the evidence of Pwsf-3, 4, 5, 7 ant 8 regarding the title and possession of the suit land, and the Appellate Court below also did not consider the same. It is further submitted that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher Ali Khan and others [57 DLR (AD) (2005) 55] held that the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment and decree of the Courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence causing failure of justice. The High Court Division is also competent to set aside the judgment and decree of the Courts below when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence, which cannot be considered as legal evidence, and had the same been not taken into consideration, the judgment and decree would not have been one as has been made. It is further contended that the High Court Division rightly found that the Appellate Court below ought to have written the impugned judgment and decree upon the independent analysis of fact and law in a comprehensive manner and, as such, there was total non-consideration of evidence by the Appellate Court below as evident from the impugned judgment and decree and, therefore, it is required that the Appellate Court below in passing the fresh judgment and decree on remand shall consider the amendments made in the plaint and find the real substance of the plaint as it contains numerous amendments and, further, consider all relevant evidence and, accordingly, the suit was rightly sent on remand to the Appellate Court below to write out a fresh judgment and decree in light of observations mate by the High Court Division. 

 14. Heard the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the material documents along with other connected papers on record. 

 16. The respondents claimed that Sam Miah by a registered deed of sale transferred one powa of land out of the 1st scheduled land to his brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique and handed over the possession to him. Thereafter, Saru Miah gifted .005 acre of land out the 1st scheduled land to Tunu Miah, son of his other brother named Kantu Miah by a registered deed of gift dated 08.12.1979 and during the field survey in the last settlement operation, the 1st scheduled land was recorded in the names of the plaintiff and his said brother according to their respective share and possession in two different khatiang and thus, the plaintiffs had been under the wrong impression that the record of rights of the land prepared naturally and legally during the field survey would be duly published. However, at same time, during the first part of baishakh, 1386 B.S., the plaintiffs upon enquiry were utterly surprised to know that the record of rights of the land described in schedule-II to the plaint which is a part And parcel of the 1st scheduled land belonged to the plaintiff in its totality, had been changed and wrongly recorded in the names of late Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah without any basis and knowledge of the plaintiff and done in the back of the plaintiff. Said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah, brother-in-law of Sheikh Selim were close relatives of the plaintiff. Having no place to live in, said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah sought for temporary shelter from the plaintiff during the time of local survey of the last settlement operation and the plaintiffs out of grace permitted them to reside in the land described in schedule-III to the plaint which is a part of the 2nd scheduled land purely for the time being on temporary basis on condition to move away therefrom after arrangement of their own accommodation elsewhere and while they were residing there on permission, said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah died leaving benind defendant Nos.1-11 and 12-14 as their legal hers respectively. Since defendant Nos.1-14 were very helpless, the plaintiff merely allowed them to reside in the 3"' scheduled land on condition to vacate the same as soon as they would be able to arrange accommodation elsewhere. Defendant No.2 purchased .01 acre of land out of the 2nd scheduled land on the western side of the land of the 3rd scheduled land. The plaintiff having learnt about the wrong and illegal record of rights of the 2nd scheduled land in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah demanded to defendant Nos.1-14 for correction of the same record of rights and asked them to vacate the land concerned and remove the structures therefrom. Though they initially agreed to take appropriate step for correction of the record, they refused to take any step later and defendant Nos.1 and 2 additionally refused to vacate the 3rd scheduled land when pressed by the plaintiff for the last time by the last part of baishakh, 1386 B.S. Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah had no title or interest of any kind in any of the lands of the suit property and as such, they recorded the land in their names by influencing the survey officials. The wrong and illegal record of rights in respect of the 2nd scheduled land cast cloud over the title of the plaintiff. 

 17. It appears from the judgment and decree of the trial Court that exhibit-1 was the saf-kabala deed whereby Saru Miah, predecessor of the present plaintiffs, owned the suit property described in schedule-I to the plaint because, by that time, there has been an acquisition of rent receiving interests under the ,East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the Zaminders remained only as superior rent receiving owner and Sam Miah purchased that entitlement from Mufti Zainuddin [exhibit-1] and at the same time, he had the occupancy right under the Government. It is admitted that the plaintiff sold a quantum of land of .71/2 acre to his younger brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique. It appears from exhibit sKaly that Sheikh Selim did not continue to stay in the house situated in the scheduled property in Longer Dewari rather after getting married for The second time, he started living with his wife in Rajar Goli, Sylhet and therefore, Sheikh Selim did not earn any right of occupancy under the landlord and so his name could not be recorded in the settlement operation. The trial Court after consideration of the evidence on record came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had occupancy right in the property described in schedule-I to the plaint and predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11/12/13 did not have title to the property described in schedule-II to the plaint by occupancy right and the defendants were in possession of the property described in schedule-II to the plaint and without a prayer for recovery of khas possession the suit is not maintainable. The trial Court also held that the suit was barred by limitation and the valuation of the suit property was not proper. The Appellate Court below without applying judicial mind concurred with the findings of the trial Court regarding dismissal of the suit and disposed of the appeal in the same tune of the trial Court. 

 18. It appears from the judgment and order of the High Court Division that the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court below ought to have given their thoughtful findings on the point of limitation on the basis of evidence on record and the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court below ought to have approached the case in proper perspective and were required to find that the plaintiff had prayed for two major reliefs: one is correction of record of rights and another is eviction of some persons from the disputed land described in schedule-III to the plaint who were claimed to be in permissive possession therein. The High Court Division further observed that the Courts below ought to have decided the ownership of the plaintiff in the actual quantum of land which remained with him after transfer. The trial Court found that "বাদিগনের সাক্ষীগনের মৌখিক সাক্ষ্য মতে বিবাদীরা আর্জির ২য় তপসিল বর্ণিত ভূমিতে বর্তমানে দখলকার আছেন। কাজেই আর্জিত ২য় তপসিল বর্ণিত সমুদয় ভূমি হইতে উচ্ছেদের প্রার্থনা ব্যতিত বাদিগনের অত্রাকারের মামলা আইনত চলিতে পারে না।" It is observed by the High Court Division that this finding of the trial Court is not quite substantial because from the 2nd scheduled land, the plaintiff did not pray for evicting any one. He wanted for correction of the record of rights only to the particular quantum of land. It was observed that the Appellate Court below ought to have written the judgment and order on the independent analysis of fact and law in a comprehensive manner. Therefore, it is required that the Appellate Court below in passing the judgment on remand would consider the amendments made in the plaint and find the real sub-stance of the plaint as it contains numerous amendments. 

 19. It reveals from the evidence on record that Pw-2 knows plaintiff-Saru Miah and his heirs and he also knows Sheikh Selim, the father of plaintiff-Saru Miah from his boyhood. It appears that, there is no allegation from defendant Nos.1-11 regarding the incorrect record of rights in the name of Saru Miah in 15 decimals of land described in schedule-I and defendant Nos.l-11 did not give any description of non-appearance of the name of Maleka Bibi in the record of rights. They only claimed that Sheikh Selim was the tenant in the 1st scheduled land and he permitted Rashid Miah to reside on 7 decimals of land described in the same schedule and after his death, his heirs had been in possession. It is admitted fact that the Zaminders filed Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Sylhet against Sheikh Selim for khas possession and eviction of them. The Zaminders obtained a decree in the aforesaid suit, but no order was passed regarding eviction and Sheikh Selim and Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique contested the suit. It appears that according to exhibit-Ka (1), Sheikh Selim left the suit land and went to Razargoli. It further appears that according to exhibit-1, Saru Miah on 22.09.1954 by a registered deed purchased the scheduled land. He sold one powa land to Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique and 0½ decimal of land to Tunu, son of Kantu Miah. 

 20. Upon perusal of the judgment of the trial Court along with the materials on record, it appears that defendant Nos.1-11 did not object to the incorrect record of rights in the name of Saru Miah in 15 decimals of land described in schedule-1 to the plaint and defencant Nos.16-24, successors of Charu Miah, another son of Sheikh Selim did not object to the claim of the plaintiff by filing written statement. The trial Court held that Rashid Miah did not have title to the land described in schedule-II to the plaint by way of settlement from the superior interest holders and there is no basis of record of rights in his name. The plaintiff and defendant Nos.1-11 admitted that the record of rights in the name of Rashid Miah is incorrect. The trial Court observed that as per the evidence of the plaintiffs witnesses predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11,Kantu Miah, had been in possession of the land described in schedule-II to the plaint with the permission of Sam Miah and there-after, defendant Nos.1-11 have been in possession Of the same with the permission of Saru Miah and the predecessor of defendant Nos.12-13, Rashid Miah, also had been in possession of the land described in schedule-II to the plaint with the permission of Sam Miah. The trial Court, however, did not categorically specify the evidence of those witnesses based on which it reached such finding. The appellate Court also did not specifically appreciate the evidence of the witnesses on record regarding the alleged permissive possession of the predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11, Kantu Miah and thereafter, that of defendant Nos.1-11 and the alleged permissive possession of the predecessor of defendant Nos. l 2-13. It is admitted that the plaintiff transferred 7 decimals of land to his brother Charu Miah. Defendant Nos.1-11 in their written statement stated that like their predecessor Kantu Miah, the heirs of Sheikh Charu got f share of the property of Sheikh Selim described in schedule-I to the plaint by way of inheritance. DW-1, vital witness of defendant Nos.1-11, during cross-examination by the plaintiff side deposed, "চারু মিয়ার ছেলেরা সারু মিয়া হইতে খরিদ সূত্রে নালিশা জমিতে দখলকার আছেন ওয়ারিশসূত্রে নয়"। This significant portion of the material evidence in the deposition of DW-1 is apparently inconsistent with the claim of defendant Nos.1-11 was overlooked both by the trial Court as well as the appellate Court. In the case of Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher All Khan and others, reported in 57DLR (AD)(2005)55, it is held that "The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse tile judgment of the Courts below when the sane has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence and the said misreading and non-consideration of the evidence caused failure of justice." In the case of Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 45, it is also held that "the High Court is empowered to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are perverse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below." 

 21. The trial Court held that the suit is barred by limitation without appreciating any evidence available on record in this regard and the appellate Court affirmed this erroneous finding without appreciating any evidence available on record in this regard. In the case of Government of Bangladesh-Vs-AKM Abdul Hye and others, 56 DLR(AD)53, it is held that "the law is now well settled that against the wrong record of rights the person whose 'interest is affected by such wrong recording need not file suit questioning legality of the record of rights so prepared and finally published within 6 years from said date or from the date of knowledge of such wrong record of rights, but he is required to file the suit seeking declaration of title within six years from the date the person-in whose name record has been wrongly prepared and finally published raises claim denying his claim on the basis of wrong record." 

 23. The High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional authority should not ordinarily reassess the evidence on record in reversing a finding of fact. In the case or Golam Sarwar (Md) and others-Vs-Md. Liakat Ali and Others reported in SODLR(AD) (1998)67, it was held that "Ordinarily, the High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional authority should not embark upon the function of the lower appellate Court to reassess the evidence on record in reversing the finding of fact. If, however, the High Court Division is satisfied that the lower appellate Court has failed to consider any material evidence in reversing a finding of fact arrived at by the trial Court upon assigning proper reason therefor, the proper course is to send back the case on remand to the appellate Court for rehearing the appeal upon proper assessment of the evidence on record."

Vs.

fulldatas.full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-respondents' case is that the suit land, schedule, "Kha" land, part of schedule "Ka" land, appertains to Taluk Fela Nyamat Fakhrunnessa Estate, a Waqf Estate, of which Jalaluddin Ahmed Miah was Mutwali. Jalaluddin settled with Syed Ahmed Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-11 schedule "KA" land in rayati right for 5 years by a registered kabuliyat dated 19.5.44, Ext.2 Jalaluddin then sold out his superior interest therein in favour of defendants No. 12, Mvi. Abu Taher Mia (respondent No. 15 herein) by a registered patta dated 8.8.52, Ext. 3, As cultivation was unprofitable, Syed Ahmed surrendered his tenancy in "Ka" schedule land by a deed of Istafanama dated 12.3.53 in favour of defendant No. 12, Ext.4, and made over possession to him. Defendant No. 12 and defendant No.13 (respondent No.16 herein) then became joint Mutwallis of Waqf Estate. They orally settled the suit `Kha' schedule land at a rental of Tk. 4.50 in rayati right in Falgoon, 1360 B.S. with the plaintiff, who has been possessing the same since then. The lease was affirmed by a Rafanama dated 3.9.68 Ext.1 between the plaintiff and the aforesaid joint Mutwallis. The plaintiff came to know that the aforesaid Syed Ahmed sold the `Kha' schedule land to Sekandar Miah, Predecessor of defendants Nos. 1-3 (present appellants) by a registered kabala dated 12.3.59 Ext. A. It is the plaintiff's case that Syed Ahmed had no saleable interest in `Kha' schdule land on 12.3.59. Kabala Ext. A was false, fraudulent and without consideration. The plaintiff also came to know that defendants Nos.1-3 filed a miscellaneous case in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Feni, under section 1/3A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against defendants Nos.4-14 for correction of record of rights. They lost the case in the trial Court but won the appeal before the District Judge, Noakhali, in Title Appeal No. 217 of 1969. The plaintiff was not made a party in the said proceeding. The suit was for a declaration of title to the 'Kha' schedule land and also for a declaration that the judgment in the aforesaid title appeal was not binding on the plaintiff. The plaintiff also pleaded adverse possession in the plaint. 

 4. The suit was decreed by the trial Court. Some of its findings, not reversed by the lower appellate Court and so noticed by the High Court Division, are that there was no assertion by the contesting defendants that Syed Ahmed did not surrender the 'Ka' schedule lands in favour of Abu Taher or that they were in possession of any land of the tenancy of Syed Ahmed. The Istafanama Ext.4 dated 12.3.53 was, therefore, accepted to be a document acted upon. As the defendants Kabala Ext. A was executed on 12.3.59 i.e. 6 years of Ext. 4, Sekandar Miah got nothing by it. The defendants failed to produce any rent receipts of Syed Ahmed or Sekander Miah to show their possession after Ext. 4. On the country, the plaintiff proved his possession of the suit; and by production of rent receipts Ext.5. The trial Court thoroughly discussed the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws. and gave a positive finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. It also held that the appellate judgment in the miscellaneous case for correction of record of right was not binding on the plaintiff, he being not a party to the same. 

 10. Apart from reiterating those submissions, Mr. M.A. Rouf, learned Counsel for the defendants-appellants, submits further that the High Court Division acted illegally by relying on the Rafanama, Ext. 1 in the absence of proof of previous approval by the Administrator of waqfs. He submits that by making the Administrator of Waqfs a party to the suit, the requirement of approval is not fulfilled. The lower appellate Court critically analysed the oral evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 and the recital of Rafanama, Ext.1 and his finding as to onus of proof, title and possession is final and conclusive and cannot be interfered with in second appeal. The plaintiff, not being a recorded tenant in the khatian, was not a necessary party in the miscellaneous case for correction of record of rights and, therefore, he was not competent to challenge the appellate judgment. Mr. Rouf finally submits that Syed Ahmed did not surrender his tenancy and the Kabala Ext. A was a bonafide transaction for valuable consideration and that the heirs of Sekandar Miah, the present appellants, are still in possession of "kha" Schedule land. Besides, the heirs of the original plaintiff Ali Azam transferred the suit land in favour of present respondents Nos. 1 and 2 during the tendency of the second appeal before the High Court Division, which fact has not been considered by the High Court Division. 

 12. It is clear that the lower appellate Court did not discuss the evidence on record with regard to possession and, therefore, its abrupt finding that the plaintiff had failed to prove his possession was rightly interfered with the trial Court's finding on possession was arrived at after full discussion of the evidence on record. We also find that the plaintiff was rightly entitled to a declaration that the appellate judgment in the proceeding for correction of record of rights was not binding on him as he was not a party thereto. It is to late in the day to claim that Syed Ahmed did not surrender the tenancy because die appellants did not join issue with the plaintiff on this score. No Court has ever found that Syed Ahmed had a saleable interest in the suit land on 12.3.59, that Ext. A was a genuine transaction for valuable consideration and Sekandar Miah or the contesting defendants were ever in possession of the suit land. The sale of the suit land by the heirs of the original plaintiff during the tendency of the second appeal will be governed by the doctrine of lis pendens and there is not much to it.

fulldatas.full_judgment:
2. The respondent instituted the above Title Suit No. 121 of 1990 praying for declaration   that the plaintiff i.e. the Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, is the owner of the suit land and that the ex parte decree dated 4.3.1975 passed by the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge), 1st Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Case No. 104 of 1974 is collusive, fraudulent, null and void stating, inter alia, that Mr. Kazi Golam Mohiuddin Faruki (G.M. Faruki) was the original owner and possessor of the suit land along with other lands and Settlement Khatian No. 4 was prepared in the name of the Court of Wards on his behalf; G.M. Faruki was permanently residing in Comilla and his house was known as "Faruki House", after partition of India in 1947 G.M. Faruki left Comilla and was living at Calcutta permanently and he also died there leaving behind no issue; one Syed Md. Barek, the predecessor of defendant No.1, was staying in the said "Faruki House" with his family and G.M. Faruki did not transfer any property to the said Syed Md. Barek; according to the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 the entire property of the G.M. Faruki vested in the Government; some part of the suit land is used as local hat/bazar and some part of it is in the possession of the Government Tahsil Office and in Dag No. 564 there is a pond which is used by the staff of the Tahsil Office and also by the shopkeepers of local hat/bazar and the employees of respondent cultivations fishery in the said pond; the respondent had also been possessing some portion of the suit land by filing up the low land and thereby improving the hat/bazar; S.A. record was wrongly prepared in the name of G.M. Faruki instead of the respondent; thereafter one Mrs. Sahera Khatoon filed Miscellaneous Case No. 104 of 1974 praying for correction of the khatian and got exparte decree dated 4.3.1975 which clouded the title of the respondent in the suit land and hence the suit. The defendant petitioner contested the above suit by filing written statement contending that late Mr. Kazi Reaz Uddin Ahmed was the owner of the suit land and he died leaving his son Nawab Sir G.M. Faruki and 5 daughters namely (1) Raheta Khatun (2) Amena Khatoon (3) Fatema Khatoon (4) Halena Khatoon (5) Shahera Khatoon as his heirs; Rahela Khatoon died leaving her only one son Syed Md. Barek as her heir; Syed Md. Barek also died leaving his two sons Syed Abdur Rahim and Syed Md. Jafor Sadek as his heirs; thereafter the said Syed Abdur Rahim died without any issue and his share devolved upon Syed Md. Jafor Sadek and thus Syed Md. Jafor Sadek became the owner and possessor of the suit property; thereafter through amicable settlement the whole property was recorded in the name of Nawab Sir G.M. Faruki along with other co-sharers of the property; a miscellaneous case filed for correction of record of right by Sahera Khatoon in which the respondent was made a party and notice of the said case was duly served upon the respondent but the respondent not being present at the time of hearing of the case on 4.3.1975, an ex parte order was passed for correction of the record and thereafter the record was duly corrected; that Syed Md. Abdur Rahim paid rent for the suit land and got receipts (Dakhilas); after the death of Syed Md. Abdur Rahmi his brother Syed Md. Jafor Sadek because the sole owner of the suit land; on 20.1.1987 the said Syed Md. Jafor Sadek transferred the suit land to Md. Shahidul Hoq, the defendant No.2 petitioner, by a registered sale deed and thus the defendant No.2/ petitioner became the owner and possessor of the suit property and none else was/is in possession of the same on behalf of the respondent. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Comilla after hearing, decreed the suit. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Artha Rin Adalat after hearing, allowed the appeal, Then the respondent moved the High Court Division whereupon Rule was issued in Civil Revision No. 4555 of 2002 and the High Court Division after hearing made the Rule absolute. 

 3. The learned counsel appearing for the defendant No. 2/ petitioner submitted that I the appellate court, the final court of facts, on consideration of the evidence and other materials on record allowed the appeal and the High Court Division failed to consider that the plaintiff respondent having failed to prove that the suit land is excess land of the landlord it cannot be said that the plaintiff respondent has right, title and interest in the suit land and as such the finding of the trial Court about the right and title of the plaintiff/respondent in the disputed land is not at all sustainable; the High Court Division also failed to consider that through amicable settlement, the suit land was recorded in the name of G.M. Faruki including other co-sharers of the property and that the respondent was made party to the Miscellaneous Case No. 104 of 1974 and notice was also served upon the respondent and the respondent not being present at the time of hearing of the case on 4.3.1975 an ex parte order was passed directing correction of the record of right and subsequently the records have been corrected. 

 4. As it appears the High Court Division on consideration of the evidence on record found that the plaintiff/respondent claimed that the suit land along with other property belonged to G.M. Faruki and during the settlement survey the suit property was shown in the custody of Court of Wards; D.W.1 in his cross examination admitted that there is no document to show that the father of G.M. Faruki was the owner of the suit property; D.W.1 also admitted that the property was recorded under C.S. Khatian No. 34 of Debiddar Mouza in the name of court of Wards on behalf of G.M. Faruki which shows that G.M. Faruki was the owner and possessor of the suit property and there is nothing on record to show that any of the sisters of G.M. Faruki ever inherited the same from their father; D.W.1 also admitted in his cross-examination that the suit property was never transferred or gifted away to any one by G.M. Faruki and he also admitted that the plaintiff respondent has taken over the property of Faruki Estate and thus the exchange of property by a deed of Ewaz has no basis; the witness of the plaintiff respondent also categorically deposed that the disputed land was vested in the Government and since G.M. Faruki left the country the plaintiff respondent is possessing the same; the High Court Division further found that the trial court disbelieved the photocopy of the rent receipts as well as the claim of possession of the defendant petitioner in the suit land and the trial court also found that although the definite case of defendant petitioner was that notice in the miscellaneous case was duly served on the plaintiff respondent but he took no steps the service of notice on consideration of both oral and documentary evidence the trial court also found that the defendant petitioner had no title or possession in the suit property and that the exparte decree obtained on 4.3.75 in the miscellaneous case was obtained by fraud; the High Court Division further found that the judgment of the trial court is well reasoned and elaborate and is amply supported by evidence and the lower appellate court failed to reverse the findings of the trial court by cognate reason; the High Court Division in its judgment also referred to the case of Md. Afaz Uddin Mollah and others vs. Md. Maizuddin Shaikh reported in BCR 1983 (AD) 48 wherein it was held that reversal of the trial court judgment without adverting to the evidence on which the trial court's judgment is based is not a proper judgment of reversal. 

 5. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the evidence and the materials on record arrived at a correct decision and there is no cogent reason to interfere with the said decision.

20. Mr TH Khan, the learned Senior Counsel appearing with Mr JN Deb and Mr Helaluddin Mollah and Mr AKM Shamsul Huq by filing affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit in opposition for the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 submitted that the property originally belonged to Khan Bahadur Abu Naser Mohammad Ahia who subsequently in the year 1922 established Waqf Estate as Waqf-ul-Lillah known as KB Ahia Waqf Estate under the approval of the then Government of Asham. Since then the case property along with other properties have been possessing and enjoying by the Waqf Estate. The Secretary, Ministry of Land, Respondent No. 2 also directed to the Deputy Commissioner of Sylhet, Maulvi Bazar, Sunamganj not to disturb the peaceful possession of the Waqf Estate and according to the said direction, the respondent No. 6 Waqf Estate filed Title Suit No. 7 of 2002 for correction of record which is still pending for determination and another Title Suit No.72 of 1999 in respect of permanent injunction was decreed in favour of the Waqf Estate against which no appeal was preferred. The petitioner has no locus standi to file instant writ petition. Facts necessary to dispose this appeal are that the appellants herein as the petitioners (hereinafter referred to as the writ-petitioners) filed the above mentioned writ petition before the High Court Division challenging Memo No. Parti: 21/97/576 dated 28-5-1997 issued by writ-respondent No.2, the Director General, Directorate of Land Record and Survey, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Tejgaon, Dhaka with a direction upon writ-respondent No.3, the Settlement Officer, Dhaka to correct the order dated 25-4-1996 passed by writ-respondent No.4, the Assistant Settlement Officer, Dhaka Southern Office of the Land Record and Survey, Tejgaon, Dhaka. 

 3. In the writ petition, it was stated, inter alia, that respondent No.5, the Capital Co-operative Housing Society Limited, as the petitioner filed Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989 before the High Court Division impleading the Director, the Settlement Office and the Assistant Settlement Officer, all of Land Records and Survey, Tejgaon, Dhaka, appellant No.1 herein (hereinafter referred to as writ-petitioner No.1) and 18 others challenging the order dated 5-2-1989 passed in Appeal Case Nos. 34046 of 1984 to 34054 of 1984 heard analogously by way of review by the Assistant Settlement Officer to have been passed without lawful authority and was no legal effect and to declare the striking out the name of the writ-petitioner (the Capital Co-operative Housing Society) from the RS Khatian No.1600(DP) as illegal and without any basis and lawful authority and also to declare the inclusion of the names of respondent Nos. 3-21 (in Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989) in the RS Khatian as fraudulent and without any basis. Subsequently, by filing a supplementary affidavit a prayer was added as to why the order dated 18-1-1989 passed by writ-respondent No.1 (a), the Settlement Officer be not declared to have been passed with-out lawful authority and was of no legal effect. 

 4. The case of the writ-respondent No.5 (in the instant writ petition) in Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989 was that the land recorded in CS Khatian Nos. 138 and 330 bearing Plot Nos.881, 890, 893, 894 with a total area of 9.46 acres land and plot Nos.878, 879 with an area of 2.86 acres land respectively within Mouza-Uttar Khan, formerly within Police Station-Keraniganj, now Police Station-Gulshan, Dhaka originally belonged to Sharafatullah who died leaving behind 4(four) sons named Abdur Rahman, Pokai, Nazimuddin, Faizuddin and one daughter named Jewar Bibi. Bhawal Raj Estate, superior landlord of the case land, got a rent decree against the said tenants for arrear of rents in respect of CS Khatian No.330 and put the decree into execution and auction purchased the lands of this khatian and got delivery of possession thereof on 20-2-1930 and the said landlord also got another decree in a title suit against the said tenants and filed an execution case for the realization of the decretal costs, attached and put the lands of CS Khatian No. 138 in Court sale, auction purchased the same and got delivery of possession thereof on 20-6-1940. Subsequently, the said landlord settled the lands of those two CS Khatians with one Rahmat Banu on 3-3-1943 and she also got her name recorded in the SA Khatian and as she was threatened to be dispossessed from the case lands, she filed Title Suit No.80 of 1965 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka for permanent injunction against the successors-in-interest of said Sharafatullah and the purchasers, but as eventually, she was dispossessed from the case land, she filed another suit being Title Suit No.9 of 1970 in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and for recovery of possession which was decreed in her favour and she got delivery of possession of the case land and later on, the said writ-petitioner purchased the entire lands from Rahmat Banu by a registered sale deed bearing No.10884 dated 24-3-1978 and got delivery of possession thereof. 

 7. On 2-4-1995, one Suruj Mea and his 28 co-sharers, on 19-4-1995, one Motiur Rahman and his two co-sharers, on 21-4-1995, one Majir uddin and another co-sharer and on 23-4-1995, Manwara Begum separately submitted four applications before respondent No.2 who directed respondent No.3 for taking legal steps upon examining those applications and in compliance with the said direction, Syed Ahammad Gazi, Assistant Settlement Officer was assigned to enquire into the matter and he submitted an enquiry report on 8-5-1995. Considering the said enquiry report, comment of the Assistant Settlement Officer and recommendation of the charge officer, it was found that there were some mistakes and irregularities in the matter of apportioning land in the draft records of rights prepared earlier, the Settlement Officer, respondent No.3 vide his order dated 17-9-1995 started Miscellaneous Case No.3439 of 1995 under rule 82A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955, in short, the Rules, 1955 in order to remove the mistakes and irregularities and to prepare correct record of right and directed Joynal Abedin Bhuiyan, Assistant Settlement Officer to submit his opinion to the Settlement Officer for approval, after hearing the matter upon giving notices on the parties. 

 8. Writ-petitioner No.2, purchased-"in-possession" from the successive heirs-in-interest of said Sharafatullah and their vendee was added as opposite party in Miscellaneous Case No.3439 of 1995 vide the order dated 8-10-1995. After receipt of the notices, all the parties concerned recorded in the said RS Khatian No. 1600(DP) and also respondent No.5 appeared in the said miscellaneous case and contested the same. After perusing the said four applications, order dated 5-2-1989 passed in the said nine appeals, the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989 and hearing the parties, Joynal Abedin Bhuiyan, the Assistant Settlement Officer, vide his order dated 2-1-1996 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.439 of 1995 proposed to prepare the RS Khatian in the names of the successive heirs-in-interest of said Sharafatullah and the petitioners along with other purchasers in possession from them after deleting the names of said Rahmat Banu and Capital Co-operative Housing Society Ltd (writ-respondent No.5 in the instant writ petition) from draft RS Khatian No.1600 and on 4-1-1996 submitted his said proposal before respondent No.3 for approval. Respondent No.3 after consulting the records vide his order dated 5-4-1996 accepted/approved the said proposal of Joynal Abedin Bhuiyan and ordered preparation of the record of right in conformity with the approved proposal and directed him to carry out the said order. Joynal Abedin Bhuiyan, vide his order dated 25-4-1996 carried out the earlier order dated 5-4-1996 passed by respondent No.3 and prepared the final RS Khatian No. 1600 of Mouza-Uttarkhan, Police Station-Gulshan Dhaka in the name of the petitioners and other successive heirs-in-interest and the purchasers-in-possession from them under rule 32 of the Rules, 1955. Thereafter the said RS Khatian No. 1600 was published finally under Rule 33 of the Rules, 1955 and a certificate stating the fact of such final publication was made by the revenue officer under rule 34(1) thereof. And then in the official Gazette Notification dated 26-9-1996, a declaration under rule 34(2) of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 was made by the Government to the effect that the records of right of Mouza-Uttar Khan, Police Station-Gulshan, Dhaka was finally published under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Following the said Gazette Notification dated 26-9-1996, respondent No.1 vide Memo No. Bhu:Ma/Sha-3/ Bhu:U :Ka/20/94/234(123) dated 6-10-1996 directed all concerned persons including respondent No.2 to take necessary steps so that fixation of LD Taxes and other functioning in this regard were done on the basis of the said finally published RS Khatians and thereby RS Khatian No.1600 was acted upon. Respondent No.5 having failed in Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989, tried to mislead and influence various authorities including the offices of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 with an intention to get extra procedural, extra statutorily and extra-judicial benefits and privileges and in course of his said improper attempts, respondent No. 2 vide his office Memo No. Prati:/21/97/576 dated 28-5-1997 passed order directing correction of the record of rights stating that an illegal order dated 25-4-1996 was passed for preparation of record of rights, when the matter was finally settled in appeal and preparation of record of rights was in the last stage of printing. The impugned Memo dated 28-5-1997 was issued without giving the writ-petitioners any chance to be heard, though the same was entirely prejudicial for them. Writ-petitioner No.2 and one Mosammat Mallika Begum being unofficially informed of the impugned order dated 28-5-1997 on 16-6-1997 submitted a memorandum to the State Minister for Land to cancel the same and the State Minister forwarded the said memorandum to writ-respondent No.2 with a direction to consult the matter with writ-petitioner No.2 who though met writ-respondent No.2, went in vain. There-after, writ-petitioner No.2 and said Mosammat Mallika Begum on 5-10-1997 submitted another memorandum to the State Minister of Land with the same prayer which was forwarded to writ-respondent No.1 vide Memo Bhu:Ma/Sha-2 (Prakalapo/17/97-503 dated 21-10-1997 with a direction for enquiry by the Director (Record), Land Record and Survey Directorate, but the said Memorandum has still been kept in abeyance. On 26-4-1998 the concerned officers visited the case land for further preparation of the record of rights thereof and they verbally informed the writ-petitioners that they were officially bound by the impugned order dated 28-5-1997 to prepare the said record of rights in accordance with the same. 

 12. Respondent Nos.6-11 got themselves added in the writ petition by filing separate petitions. Added respondent No.6, Syed Golam Mostafa filed an affidavit-in-opposition to contest the Rule contending, inter alia, that the case land belonged to Bhawal Courts of Wards. One Sharafatullah took settlement of that land from Bhawal Estate; Bhawal Estate instituted Rent Suit No.2525 of 1927 for arrears of rent; that suit was decreed; thereafter the Bhawal Courts of Wards purchased the suit land in auction in Rent Execution Case No.373 of 1928 on 20-2-1930; Bhawal Court of Wards got possession of the land through Court on 20-2-1930; Bhawal Court of Wards thereafter settled the land with Rahmat Banu on 22-3-1943; legal heirs of Sharafatullah filed Title Suit No.652 of 1930 challenging the aforesaid auction; that the said suit was dismissed on contest on 10-9-1930; that the legal heirs of Sharafatullah filed Title Appeal No.1011 of 1930 on 17-3-1931 which was also dismissed; thereafter the plaintiff of Title Suit No.652 of 1930 filed Second Appeal No.2927 of 1931 before the High Court Division which was also dismissed; thus auction purchase was confirmed by all the three Courts; that one Zewar Bibi, daughter of Sharafatullah filed Title Suit No.113 of 1946 for declaration of title; that the suit was dismissed on 6-1-1948; Zewar Bibi filed another suit being Title Suit No.31 of 1950 renumbered as Title Suit No.72 of 1951; that suit was dismissed on 19-4-1952; that on 22-12-1964 Zewar Bibi filed title appeal (number is not available from the record) against the aforesaid judgment which was also dismissed; accordingly, the land was recorded in the name of Rahmat Banu who took settlement from the landlord auction purchaser; the heirs of Sharafatullah took barga of the case land from Rahmat Banu; since the Bargadars stopped giving barga paddy to Rahmat Banu, she filed Title Suit No.9 of 1970 against Asia Khatun and others (legal heirs of Sharafatullah); that suit was decreed on 22-8-1972; that Rahmat Banu got possession in Title Execution Case No.6 of 1973. The Bargadars filed First Appeal No.6 of 1976 before the High Court Division; that appeal was dismissed on 30-4-1975 for non prosecution, thus title of Rahmat Banu was again reaffirmed; that on 23-3-1978 Rahmat Banu by a registered sale deed sold the case land to Capital Co-operative Society, i.e. respondent No.5; that respondent No.5 being a developer developed the case lands, divided the same into 155 plots and distributed those to 155 members who constructed pucca and semi pucca residential houses and have been residing in those houses; that in pursuance of the aforesaid registered sale deeds, the respondents and the other allottees got their names duly mutated and paid rents to the Government upto 1996, but because of the dispute as mentioned in earlier paragraphs the Government was not taking any ground rent from the allottees. 

 13. Writ-petitioner No. 1 (appellant No.1) filed a supplementary affidavit stating, inter alia, that the original owner of the land of CS Khatian No.330 of Mouza 195, Uttar Khan under present Police Station-Uttar Khan was one Bholanath Singh and from whom Sharafatullah, son of late Robiullah became the owner and possessor under sthitiban rayoti title in respect of Plot Nos. 878, 879, 881, 890, 89. 994 measuring in total 12.32 acres land and the name of Sharafatullah was correctly recorded in CS Khatian Nos.138 and 330. After the death of CS recorded tenant, Sharafatullah, the name of one Rahmat Banu appeared in SA Khatian Nos. 239 and 434 in respect of the aforesaid 12.32 acres land appertaining to those six plots and, as such, the heirs of Sharafatullah at the time of last RS operation filed 9(nine) objection cases under rule 30 of the Rules, 1955 and those objection cases were allowed in part. Respondent No.5 (Capital Co-operative Housing Society Ltd) being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order passed in the aforesaid 9(nine) objection cases filed 9 (nine) appeals under Rule 31 of the Rules, 1955 bearing numbers: 34046-34054 of 1984 and on consideration of the papers and documents those appeals were finally dismissed on contest by the Assistant Settlement Officer, Dhaka Zone, Dhaka by his order dated 5-2-1989 with a direction to record the names of the objector appellants only in RS Khatian No.1600. As it appeared from annexure-' Ka', respondent No.5 settled the properties of SA Khatian Nos.239 and 434 covering 6 plots of original CS Khatian Nos.138 and 330 measuring 12.32 acres land by way of perpetual lease to 162 persons and after they lost in the settlement appeals under rule 31 being Nos.3446-3454 of 1948, filed Writ Petition No. 1080 of 1989 and obtained a Rule Nisi; the Rule Nisi issued in the aforesaid writ petition was discharged on 2-3-1993; Another Division Bench by its judgment and order dated 14-11-1991 in Writ Petition Nos.207 and 208 of 1989 dealing with more or less the same principle of law involved in Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989, amongst others, declared that the Director General of Land Records could not exceed his power by entertaining and disposing of a second review petition against the order passed by the Settlement Officer in appellate jurisdiction in respect of correction of record of rights. Respondent No.5 did not challenge the judgment and order dated 2-3-1993 passed in Writ Petition No.1080 of 1989 before this Division and thus accepted the result of their above mentioned writ petition, but got a series of suits filed through their lessees before the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka impleading the writ-petitioners as defendant Nos.27 and 34 respectively and respondent No.5 as pro-forma defendant No.55. Writ-petitioner No.2 was contesting those suits by filing written statements and to the knowledge of the petitioners, respondent No.5 was giving active support and assistance to the plaintiffs of those ongoing title suits in which they challenged the Gazette being No. ভুঃ মঃ/শাঃ-২(গঃ বিঃ)-৭৪-৯৫-৩৯২ dated 24-9-1996 in respect of RS Khatian No. 1600 more or less attracting the subject matter of the writ petition. 

 "Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners submit-ted that after preparation and final publication and gazette notification of khatian on completion of all legal requirements as provided in State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the State Acquisition Rules, 1955 there was no scope for the respondent No.2 to reopen the issue on any pretext and in these circumstances, the High Court Division seriously erred in law in holding that the impugned memo is merely a communication from one office to another to perform certain official acts and committed gross injustice in discharging the Rule on the ground of maintainability alone without going to the merit of the case; that after publication of the official gazette notification under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 read with Rule 34(2) of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955, the record of right is to be presumed to be correct under Rule 35 of the said State Acquisition Rules which can only be declared incorrect by the competent memo issued by the respondent No.2 is without jurisdiction and is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect; that all the necessary parties were made parties in the writ petition and, as such, the case law referred to by the High Court Division are not applicable in the present case. The learned Counsel further submitted that having regard to the provision of rule 42 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1955 which vested the Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' with the power to direct cancellation of any portion of the proceedings referred to in rules 28 to 30 in respect of any district or part of a district or local area at any time before publication of the final record of rights, the High Court Division was wrong in failing to hold that the impugned order passed by the respondent No.2 after publication of the gazette notification dated 24-9-1999 under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which is final, directing the Settlement Officer to correct the record of right in favour of respondent No.5 upon finding that the direction dated 24-4-1996 to publish the record of rights in the name of the petitioner and others, ultra vires, the provision of the said rule 42 and is without lawful authority, arbitrary and malafide." 

 19. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the High Court Division discharged the Rule Nisi on the findings, inter alia, that: (i) The interest of the writ-petitioners (there were two writ-petitioners) in the case land was not stated in the writ petition; it was not clear what quantum of land belonged to each of them "singularly and/or jointly" and how they would be aggrieved if the survey records were amended pursuant to the impugned Memo; (ii) the impugned memo did not contain any quantum of land or mention any specific plot number or khatian number except referring to the land "as that recorded in the name of Capital Co-operative Housing Society Limited in Mouza-Uttar Khan"; (iii) the occupants and the owners of the land in question had not been made parties, if the Rule Nisi was made absolute as prayed for by the appellants, then all the persons in possession of the concerned land and the persons who claimed title thereof would be adversely affected. They also had a right to be heard before any order could be passed affecting their interest in the land, no one except certain officials connected with the Land Record and Survey and Capital Co-operative Housing Society Limited represented by its Chairman were made respondents; (iv) the appellants impugned memo No.Prati:21/97/576 dated 28-5-1997 issued under the signature of writ-respondent No.2, Director General, Directorate of Land Record and Survey, Tejgaon, Dhaka addressed to the Settlement Officer. Dhaka regarding correction of records in Mouza-Uttar Khan in the name of Capital Co-operative Housing Society Limited stating that the land survey records prepared as per rules in the name of Capital Co-operative Housing Society Limited was at the last stage for publication; that after hearing the appeal through an illegal order dated 25-4-1996 under rule 42 of the Rules, 1955, an order was passed for recording the said land in the name of some other persons; the Director General, Land Records and Survey, after enquiry found the said order illegal and gave direction for correction of the survey records as per the rules; (v) the impugned Memo was merely a communication from one office to another to perform certain official acts and that was not acted upon. 

 22. The impugned memo was annexed to the writ petition as annexure-'F'. A perusal of the same shows that the same was not communicated to the writ-petitioners and it was a correspondence made by the Director-General of the Land Records and Land Survey, the Government of Bangladesh, Tejgaon to one of its Settlement Officer. In the writ petition, the writ-petitioners also made statements that—"As the writ-petitioners were not served upon any copy of the said memo dated 28-5-1997 they collected an attested copy thereof from the office of the respondent No. 1 and the same is annexed hereto and marked as annexure-'F'." From the above statements, it is clear that the impugned memo was not communicated to the writ-petitioners. Internal correspondence unless communicated to the person concerned cannot be the basis of cause of action for moving the High Court Division under its power of judicial review and we hold that since the copy of the impugned memo was not communicated to the writ-petitioners, no cause of action arose to seek any remedy challenging the said Memo.

And government granted long term lease of the same to one Alizan on 17-08-1960, who was in possession therein by constructing homestead. Alizan on obtaining permission in writing from the Government transferred the suit land to the appellant by a registered kabala dated 17-03-1985. Subsequently, the appellant mutated his name in the records of right and had been in peaceful possession by constructing house in the land in suit and also paid rent to contiguous east of the suit land there was a standing house of the respondent. The respondent with the help of some unruly persons on 13-06-1986 attempted to dispossess the appellant from the land in suit. Although the attempt was unsuccessful due to intervention of the local people yet the respondent continued to threat to dispossess the petitioner from the land. 

 3. Respondent contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made by the petitioner. His case was that the suit was barred by limitation and was bad for defect of parties. His further case was that the suit property originally belonged to Kalidas Mukherjee and C.S. khatian No. 82 stood in his name. Kalidas Mukherjee transferred the land to Mirza Fazlul Karim by a pitta dated 22-06-1931. Fazlul Karim by a deed of trust dated 30-05-1932 created a trust in respect of .03 1/2 acre of the land of Plot No. 106 and .22 decimals of C.S. Plot No. 105 of Mouja Jessore. On the trust land a Lilla boarding, an Orphanage and a Muslim Library and a Madrasha were also established. And respondent is running the same. As the trust land was illegally recorded in the name of the Government, the respondent filed Suit No. 26 of 1985 for correction of the record, which is pending. The respondent's further case was that the petitioner neither had title nor possession in the land in suit. 

 "Because the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the concurrent findings of the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court, based on due consideration of the evidence on record and free from any error of law occasioning a failure of justice." 

 5. Mr. Shaikh Razzaque Ali, the learned counsel appearing the for appellant, having raised the only point as noted above, argued that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the concurrent finding of the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court based on the consideration of evidence on record and free from any error of law occasioning failure of justice. 

 7. Mr. Nawab Ali, the learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the respondent No.1 (a), on the other hand, contended that the suit land recorded in C.S. khatian No. 82 originally belonged to Kalidas Mukherjee while he was in possessing having had the right, title interest transferred the same by a registered patta dated 22-06-1931 in favour of Mirza Fazlul Karim, who later on established a Trust namely 'Muslim Trust' by registered trust deed dated 30-05-1932 in respect of .3½ decimals of land of C.S. Plot No. 106 and .22 decimals of C.S. Plot No. 105 of Mouza-Jessore wherein the said Fazlul Karim established a Lillah Boarding, an Orphanage and a Muslim Library in the suit land. Subsequently, the Madrasha was also established therein. He further pointed out the suit land has been recorded in S.A. Plot No. 105 under Khatian No.1 in the name of Government of which the defendant-respondents already filed Title Suit No. 26 of 1985 for correction of his alleged wrong record. Mr. Nawab Ali has, however, empathically argued that the aforesaid two registered deeds clearly proved that the defendant-respondent is very much in possession of the suit land and for wrong record, he has already filed the above-mentioned Title Suit for correction of said record in the name of the Government. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, the plaintiff could neither challenge the aforesaid two registered deeds by properly framed suit in any Court of law, rather possession was very much in favour of said Fazlul Karim. He submits that the High Court Division having considered the registered documents as well as other evidence on record rightly set aside the impugned judgments and decrees of the Courts below. 

 8. We have perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division as well as the judgments of the Courts below. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and evidence on record, we are of the view that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division having applied its judicial mind came to following findings: 

 9. It is settled law that the plaintiff must prove his case to the effect that he purchased the suit land from Alizan who got the land on the basis of lease taken from the Government though the record of right have been made in the name of the Government is the S.A. record. But the correctness of the S.A. record is under challenge by the defendant in Title Suit No. 26 of 1985. Therefore, we find that the plaintiff-respondent failed to establish his prima-faice title and possession in the suit land and such both the courts below committed an error of law resulting in an error in their decisions causing failure of justice.
