2. It is stated in the writ petition that the petitioner's father acquired the property in question measuring 3.33 acres of land in Khatian No. 2 under Sylhet Municipality by purchase on 12th Chaitra, 1354 BS by a registered Kabala. But since the respondent No.4. Lacca Tura Tea Estate illegally took over possession and managed to record the same in its name in the record of rights, father of the petitioner filed Title Suit No. 371 of 1963 in the First Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet against the Ministry of Land and Lacca Tura Tea Estate and others for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in respect of the said land along with other lands. The said suit was decreed in part declaring title only in favour of the father of the petitioner in respect of the second schedule land by judgment and decree dated 27-2-1973 against which the respondent Nos.l and 4, namely, the Ministry of Land and Lacca Tura Tea Estate, preferred Title Appeal No. 100 of 1973 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet. Similarly, the father of the petitioner preferred cross appeal, Title Appeal No. 76 of 1973, as the trial Court failed to pass a decree for recovery of khas possession regarding the second schedule land and also for not making the commission Report, Map, etc part of the decree. Title Appeal No. 100 of 1973 filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 4 was dismissed and Title Appeal No. 76 of 1973 was allowed by judgment and decree dated 8-9-1983. During pendency of the aforesaid appeal petitioner's father died and accordingly, his three brothers and mother impleaded themselves as appellants. Thereafter, the petitioner and his co-owners filed Title Execution Case No.5 of 1984 and ultimately, obtained possession of the land on 8-3-1984 through Court by executing the decree. After conclusion of the said execution case the mother of the petitioner died leaving behind the petitioner and his three brothers and of them, two died unmarried and the third died leaving behind one daughter and the said daughter transferred-her share in favour of the petitioner and delivered possession thereof. The petitioner thus became the sole owner in possession of the suit land. The heirs of the respondent No.4 in Title Appeal No. 76 of 1973 however, preferred two revisional applications being Civil Revision Nos.161 and 162 of 1984 before the High Court Division. Ultimately, the Rules in the aforesaid two revisional applications were discharged by the judgment and order dated 3-9-1987. The said heirs then filed two Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 245 and 246 of 1988 before the Appellate Division which were also dismissed by judgment and order dated 27-1-1991. 

 3. Accordingly, the petitioner filed Mutation Case No. 107/83-84 before the Revenue Deputy Collector Sylhet under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for correction of record of rights in his favour in pursuance of the aforesaid judgment and decrees passed by the highest Court of the country. But the Revenue Deputy Collector stayed the matter. Hence the petitioner preferred Mutation Appeal No. 95 of 1990 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet, who heard and allowed the said appeal with direction to record the name of the petitioner. The petitioner thereafter filed Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1991 before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Sadar, Sylhet for correction of the record of rights. The Assistant Commissioner (Land) thereafter by order dated 23-1-1994 approved mutation in favour of the petitioner and consequently, a separate khatian was opened in the name of the petitioner. 

 4. The respondent No. 4 Lacca Tura Tea Estate, thereupon, preferred Mutation Appeal No. 22 of 1994 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet against the order passed by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) asserting that the land in question was a vested property and, as such, it took settlement of the same from the Government and it was therefore rightly recorded in its name in the record of right. The petitioner having received notices of the said mutation appeal, contested the same submitting all papers, namely, the judgments and decrees passed by the Civil Courts including the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court declaring title of the petitioner thereto and giving possession. But the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) by the impugned order dated 3-6-1998. Annexure-I, forwarded the case record to the Ministry of Land without giving any decision either allowing or rejecting the mutation. Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) while forwarding the record to the Ministry observed the Lacca Tura Tea Estate was the owner and possessor of the land in question on the basis of settlement by the Government and there was no scope of mutation in favour of the petitioner. He also mentioned in the aforesaid order that there were two title suits pending in respect of the land in question by two other private individuals and without disposal of the said suits and without the results of the said suits being submitted to the Ministry there was no scope to pass any mutation order. 

 7. It is noted from the record that the petitioner in order to establish his right, title and interest in the land in question and for recovery of khas possession thereof filed a civil suit being Title Suit No. 371 of 1963 and obtained the decree in his favour which was finally affirmed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. The dispute with regard to the title and possession of the land in question between the parties, namely, the Government of Bangladesh, Lacca Tura Tea Estate and the petitioner should therefore be taken to have been finally resolved. The petitioner therefore started a Mutation case under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for mutation of his name by removing the name of the Government and/or Lacca Tura Tea Estate in the record of right on the basis of the aforesaid decrees. The petitioner eventually obtained necessary Mutation order on 23-1-199.4 in his favour by the Assistant Commissioner (Land) in Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1991 and in pursuance thereto a separate khatian was opened in his name. The respondent No.4 Lacca Tura Tea Estate thereupon filed a Mutation Appeal No. 22 of 1984 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) whereupon the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dragged on with the matter for 4 years and then without deciding the matter himself forwarded the case record regarding the mutation to the Ministry of Land by the impugned order dated 3-6-1998 with the observation as stated above. 

 8. Since the petitioner sought correction of the record of right by mutating his name in respect of the land in question on the strength of the final judgment and decree of the highest Civil Courts of the country he rightly approached the Revenue Deputy Collector by filing an application under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 54 reads as under: 

 "The Revenue-officer shall make such alteration in the records-of-rights or the Compensation Assessment Roll as may be necessary to give effect to any directions issued by the Commissioner or other officer under section 49 or an order made by a Special Judge under section 51 or section 53 or under sub-section" (4) of section 52 or to any final order or decree of a Civil Court of the High Court Division passed in any suit, appeal or proceeding declaring tide to and, or possession of any land." 

 9. When the matter was subsequently brought before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) he was required in law to decide the matter either giving a decision instead of forwarding the same to the Ministry of Land by giving unwarranted and illegal observations. Since the question of title and possession have been settled by the highest Court of the country the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) had, in fact, no option in law but to mutate the name of the petitioner by correcting the record of right: The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) not only acted without jurisdiction in sending the matter to the Ministry of Land without deciding the matter himself with untenable observations but also did so in colourable exercise of his official power. The impugned order dated 3-6-1998 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Sylhet is therefore declared to have been passed without any lawful authority.

2. Complainant-opposite Party No.1 made a complaint before, the court of Magistrate, Tangail against accused petitioners alleging, inter alia, that they in collusion with each other created a forged order purported to be made by then Munsif, 3rd Court, Tangail in Miscellaneous Case No.337 of 1973 under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the Act, for correction of the record of right in respect of the case land, that subsequently the petitioners filed the said forged order before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Mirzapur for correcting the record of rights in their favour, that pursuant thereto, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued notice upon the complainant who on enquiry ascertained that petitioners filed a forged copy of the order of the learned Munsif and thereupon filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) for attaching the said forged order of the learned Munsif for drawing up a proceeding under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) refused to make any complaint and directed the complainant to file case against the accused and accordingly, complaint was made. 

 5. Mr Md Amjad Hossain, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1, on the other hand, submits that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) while initiating a proceeding of mutation of the record-of-rights is not a Revenue Court within meaning of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore, there is no legal bar in making a complaint by a private person against petitioners in respect of a forged Judgment produced by them for mutation of their names before the Revenue Officer. In support of his contention, learned Advocate has referred a decision in the case of Idris Ali and another vs State 38 DLR 270. 

 8. Now the question is a Revenue Officer, in the instant case Assistant Commissioner (Land), dealing with a Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court within the meaning of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shortly the Code. In the Code, no definition of the "Revenue Court" has been given. Since there is no definition of Revenue Court in the Code, let us examine other Laws as to the meaning of the term 'Revenue Court. In the Tenancy Law i.e. the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there is no definition of Revenue Court." The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act only speaks of "Revenue Officer" includes "any officer whom the government may appoint to discharge all or any of the functions of a Revenue officer under this Act or any rules made thereunder". Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 provide the procedure of preparation of the records of rights by the Revenue officer. Sub- section 9(a) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act defines the term "Chief Revenue Officer" means the National Board of Revenue constituted under the National Board of Revenue Order 1972, (president's Order 76 of 1972). Since there is no definition of "Revenue Court" in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the General Clauses Act let us examine the meaning of the term "Court." Section 6 of the Code describes classes of criminal Courts, namely: 

 143. Maintainability of the Record-of- rights. The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of-rights prepared or revised under part IV, or under this part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of-(a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance; 

 For carrying out purposes of the Act, the Government promulgated the Tenancy Rules 1954 in exercise of powers conferred under section 152 of the Act. In the said Rules, Rules 22 and 23 provide the procedures and the manner in which the record of rights referred to In section 143 shall be maintained. The relevant portions of Rules 22 and 23 are reproduced below- 

 (4) "In the case of apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of-rights, the report shall state the mouza and Khatian number of the holding to which such mistakes relate. 

 2(1) The Revenue-officer shall, if he is vested with necessary powers in this behalf under the Act, incorporate, and, if he is not vested with such powers, send up proposals to the officer vested with such powers for incorporating necessary changes in the record-of-rights,- 

 (3) The Revenue-Officer shall, either on application or on receipt of a report under sub-rule (1) of rule 22, for the correction of apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of- rights, after consulting the previous settlement records and making such other enquiries as he considers necessary, direct correction of such clerical mistakes, 

 (4) The Revenue-officer shall, either on application or on receipt of a report under clause (i) of sub-rule (1), for the correction of an entry and making such other enquiries as he considers necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry, and his act in doing so being a ministerial act, shall not be open to appeal. 

 13. These Rules clearly provide that when Tahsilder primarily responsible for. report to the Revenue Officer apparently makes clerical mistake in record-of-rights, changes of ownership, etc., the Revenue Officer shall direct correction of such clerical mistakes and making such inquiries as he "may consider necessary direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act being a ministerial act shall not be open to appeal. A Revenue Officer holding an inquiry in a mutation proceeding, in the premises, does not become a court as he does not really adjudicate a right and he does not give a decision which is binding on the parties. He merely corrects apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of-rights and directs correction of such clerical mistakes. If he is vested with necessary powers, incorporates necessary changes in the record-of-rights mutating the names when mutation is asked for as a result of inheritance on the report of Tahsilder under Rule 22 and also when mutation is asked for as a result of transfer, his acts being ministerial acts, shall not be open to appeal as provided in Rule 23 sub-rule (4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1954. He certainly exercises no judicial function. The functions are much more in the nature of a fiscal enquiry for the purpose of ascertaining which of the several claimants for the occupation of certain denominations of immovable property may be put into occupation of it with greater confidence than the revenue for which will be paid. Inquiry in mutation proceedings, therefore, being a fiscal inquiry conducted by agents of the State, for their own purposes, it could by no means be described as judicial proceeding. Therefore, a Revenue Officer when dealing with a mutation proceedings does not constitute a "Revenue Court" within the wider meaning of section 195(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 "We respectfully disagree with the above views of the Division Bench which held that Revenue Officer doing mutation matter is not a Revenue Court. Tenancy Rules 30 and 31 deal with preparation of record-of-rights and Tenancy Rules 20-24 deal with correction of records of right by way of Mutation. Both the matters are dealt with by the Revenue Officers and regarding Mutation matter there is a provision for review to the Revenue Officer. Weare of the view that the principle applicable to preparation of record of right also be applicable to the mutation of name in the record of rights inasmuch as both relate to preparation, modification, addition or alteration of record of rights. Relying upon the principles as laid down by the Appellate Division in above decision reported in BCR 1987 (AD) 152, we hold that the Revenue Officer dealing in Mutation of the name in the record of rights is also a Revenue Court. As we are holding this view relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division, we need not refer this matter to a Full Bench for our disagreement with another Division Bench." 

 17. In the Appellate Division's case the issue was whether an Objection Officer having power of an Assistant Settlement Officer in deciding Objection Petition is a Revenue Court or not. The Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 held that a Revenue Officer having additional powers of Settlement Officer while hearing objection case shall have all powers exercisable by a civil court in a trial of suits under Civil Procedure Code and decides ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land and therefore, the objection officer is functioning as a "Revenue Court". These Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose and the manner in which revision of the record-of-rights can be prepared under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 144 provides: 

 "(1) The Government may in any case if it thinks fit make an order directing that a record-of-rights in respect of any district, part of a district or local area be prepared or revised by a Revenue Officer in accordance with such rules as may be made by the Government in this 

 (7) When all such objections and appeals have been considered and disposed of according to such rules as the Government may make in this behalf, the Revenue-Officer shall finally frame the record and shall cause such record to be finally published in the prescribed manner and the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly prepared or revised under this section. 

 "29 Publication of draft record of rights: 

 objection regarding the ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land shall be decided summarily by the Revenue Officer. The record shall contain a brief summary of the evidence taken and abstract of the reasons for the decision. Objections shall not be disposed of in the absence of any of the parties naturally interested or their representatives, unless the Revenue Officer be satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, in writing, that the notice was duly served on the person concerned. 

 (2) Before passing the final order on any such appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. 

 "35 Presumption as to the correctness of record-of-rights: (1) When a record of rights is finally published under rule 33, the publication shall be conclusive evidence that the record has been duly revised under section 144 of the Act." 

 These rules are included in chapter VII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 under the heading "Revision of record of rights under section 144 of the Act." This chapter deals with the particulars to be recorded at the stages of the work, procedure of work up to attestation, publication of draft record of rights, objection, appeal, publication of final records, certificate of final publication, presumption as to correctness of record of rights, powers of Revenue Officers, etc. while revising the record-of-rights under section 144 of the Act. After such revision of the record-of-rights at the instance of the Government of any district, part of a district or local area by the Revenue Officer appointed for the purpose who shall have either with or without the additional designation of "Settlement Officer", or "Assistant Settlement Officer", such Revenue Officer shall publish a draft record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection at such convenient place as he may determine and a proclamation be published informing the tenants/maliks for filing objections. After hearing the objections, if any, he shall proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. Similarly, in case of an appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. The provisions of Act and the Rules clearly show that the revision of the record-of-rights made under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has' presumptive value, but any order of mutation of the record made under section 143 of the Act has no such presumptive value. A Revenue Officer appointed with the power of Settlement Officer shall have all powers exercisable by a Civil Court in the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure. These Rules and the rules framed by the Governor in Council of Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 are closely akin Rule 36 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 is similar to Rule 41 of the Bengal Rules. Similarly, Rules 39 and 40 are equivalent to Rules 44 and 45 of Bengal Rules. The Bengal Government Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose of chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It is settled that the record of rights prepared in chapter I of the Bengal Tenancy Act i.e. under sections 101-104 of the Bengal Tenancy Act have the presumptive value as in section 144 of the Act but such presumption is not available in section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the Appellate Division's case no argument was made as to whether a Revenue Officer dealing with Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court or not and naturally the Appellate Division has not decided the said issue. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed is quite distinguishable from the facts of the case of Idris Ali (38 DLR 270) and the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (44 DLR 533). The Appellate Division case was decided upon consideration of the Rules contained in Chapter VII and VIII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 which were framed in exercise of section 152(2)(2b) of the Act, for carrying out the purposes for all or any of the provisions of section 144 of the Act which the facts in the case of Idris Ali (Supra) and that of Ajit Kumar Sarkar(Supra) are similar to the present case, which relate to mutation proceedings under section 143 of the Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 framed in exercise of section 152 (2)(2a) of the Act. In the premises aforesaid, we are in respectful agreement with the views taken by the Division of the High Court Division in the case of Idris Ali (Supra). For the reasons discussed above and the provisions of law quoted herein before, with due respect to the learned Judges of the High Court Division, we are unable to endorse the views taken by them in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (Supra). 

 "Where a Division Bench of the High Court is inclined to take a different view from that declared in an earlier judgment of a similar Division Bench one course open to the Court was to "have expressed their doubts regarding the view taken in the precedent case a Court of co-equal jurisdiction, while yet following that view, and left the matter to be raised in appeal before this Court (Supreme Court)" A single judge or a Division Court possesses the full force of a decision of the High Court, and is subject only to modification or correction by proper appeal to the Supreme Court, except in the few cases where provision is made by the Letters Patent for an appeal or other mode of variation within the High Court, in which case the latter decision would possess the full force of a decision by the High Court, and would be amenable to appeal by this Court." 

 23. Send down the lower court records.

2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the CS recorded tenants, namely Kalipada Karmakar and Jitendra Nath Karmakar, filed Rent Suit no. 1785 of 1950 for recovery of arrears of rents against two full brothers, namely Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal and Md. Abdul Latif Mondal, in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkhira on 27.09.1950 and through a compromise agreement (Solenama) Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal got 3/4 share and his brother Abdul Latif Mondal got 1/4 share of 15.08 acres of land. On 05.04.1956 Md. Abdul Latif Mondal sold out his above 1/4 share i.e. entire 4.00 annas shares of the above entire 15.08 acres of land by the registered sale deed no. 2036 dated 05.04.1956 to Most. Hasne Banu, Most. Futfuti, Most. Bedana and Most. Kamala. Out of above 3/4 share i.e. 12.00 annas share of the entire 15.08 acres of land, Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal gifted .50 annas share of land to his brother’s daughter Ambia Khatun and, accordingly, in the SA Khatian no. 452, 11.50 annas share was recorded in the name of Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal, .50 annas share was recorded in the name of Ambia Khatun and 4.00 annas share was recorded in the names of Hasne Banu, Futfuti Bibi, Bedana Bibi and Kamala Bibi being 1.00 anna for each of them. Thereafter, Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal sold his remaining entire share of 11.50 annas, which is 10.33 acres of land, to the petitioner by the registered sale deed no. 5363 dated 03.06.1985 and, pursuant to the said transfer on 03.10.1985, the Mutation Case no. 380(IX-I)/85-86 was filed before the Assistant Commissioner of Debhatta Land Office (hereinafter referred to as the A/C Land, Debhatta) and vide the order dated 15.10.1985 the mutation was done in favour of the petitioner and, accordingly, the SA Khatian no. 233/2 was prepared in the name of the petitioner in respect of 10.33 acres of land. It is stated that after creation of the SA Khatian no. 233/2, the petitioner conjointly with Bedana Bibi, Kamala Bibi sold 40 decimals of land to one Abdul Gaffur Gazi under the record shown in the SA Khatian no. 233/2. 

 3. On 05.05.2005, Mst. Futfuti Bibi, Mst. Bedana @ Vejali Bibi, Mst. Kamala Bibi and others filed Title Suit no. 25 of 2005 before the Assistant Judge, Debhatta, Satkhira against the petitioner and others praying for partition and cancellation of the petitioner’s aforesaid deed no. 5363 dated 03.06.1985 when the plaint of the aforesaid suit was returned by the said Court under Order 7 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure (shortly, the CPC) by the order dated 25.03.2013. Subsequently, on 20.06.2013 the same was instituted in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Satkhira and was renumbered as Title Suit no. 50 of 2013 which is still pending. Thereafter, Mst. Futfuti Bibi, Bedana Bibi, Kamala Bibi and Amina Bibi filed an application to the A/C Land, Debhatta and the said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case no. 02/08-09 under Section 149 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act, 1950 and (hereinafter referred to as the SAT Act) for review of the order passed in Mutation Case no. 380/85-86 with a prayer for cancellation of the petitioner’s mutation and, thereby, to restore the previous status of the mutation with six names as was recorded in the SA Khatian no. 233. The above review application was rejected on 18.05.2009 and against the said order they moved the Collector who, by his order dated 28.12.2011, registered their representation as Miscellaneous Appeal no. 47 of 2010 and allowed the same. Against the aforesaid order dated 28.12.2011 the petitioner filed Miscellaneous Appeal no. 25 of 2011 before the Divisional Commissioner, Khulna who dismissed it by his order dated 31.02.2012. Against the said order the petitioner filed Appeal no. 5-06/2013 (Mutation), Satkhira before the Land Appeal Board and the same was dismissed on 17.04.2014. Against which the petitioner filed a review case being no. 5-08/2014 (Mutation) Full Board, Satkhira and the Full Board dismissed the said review case by its order dated 18.05.2014. 

 5. Respondent nos. 7 to 9 contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that the total land under the SA Khatian no. 233 is 15.08 acres and there were 6 (six) recorded owners and each of them had equal share of 2.51 acres of land. It is claimed that Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal was entitled to have a share of 2.51 acres of land only under the SA Khatian no. 233 and, accordingly, he did not have any right and title to sell 10.33 acres of land. It is alleged that the statements regarding Rent Suit no. 1785 of 1950 are concocted as no such a suit had ever been instituted by the CS recorded tenants against Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal and Md. Abdul Latif Mondal and, further, no Solenama was ever made between the said CS recorded tenants and the two brothers and the judgment and decree dated 27.09.1950 is a forged and fraudulent one. It is further alleged that the registered deed no. 5363 dated 03.06.1985 is also a forged one. It is claimed that the Mutation Case no. 380(IX-1)/85-86 was allowed by the A/C Land, Debhatta without issuing any notice to all the recorded owners of the SA Khatian no. 233. It is stated that the petitioner and respondent nos. 7-10 are 12 brothers and sisters and they have some other paternal land properties and since it was necessary for partition and declaration of title of the property among them, the Partition Suit no. 25 of 2005 was instituted initially in a Court which did not have jurisdiction to entertain the said suit and subsequently the said suit was filed in a competent Court. It is stated that the Collector had rightly allowed the appeal of these respondents and, thereafter, the Divisional Commissioner, then, the Land Appeal Board had correctly dismissed the appeals and, finally, vide the impugned order the Full Board of the Land Appeal Board also rightly dismissed the review case. 

 7. Mr. Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, at the very outset, takes us through the impugned order in tandem with the preceding orders thereto namely, the orders passed by the A/C Land, Debhatta of Satkhira, the Collector (Additional Deputy Commissioner) of Satkhira and the Divisional Commissioner of Khulna and submits that while the order passed by the A/C Land appears to be in consonance with the provisions of the SAT Act, the subsequent orders passed by the appellate authorities namely, the Collector (the Additional Deputy Commissioner), the Divisional Commissioner and finally the Land Appeal Board, are beyond the provisions of the SAT Act. In an endeavor to elaborate his submission on this point, he places Section 143 of the SAT Act and submits that the Collectors and all other Revenue Officers, while performing the functions of mutation, subdivision, amalgamation etc, are carrying out executive nature of jobs/tasks and their duty is only to record the names of the present tenants as per the papers and information presented to them by the Tahshilders or as per the information provided by the applicant. He continues to submit that in the case at hand, however, the appellate authorities have exceeded their jurisdictions in directing the A/C Land to apportion the shares of the owners of the case land and then mutate their names against their respective shares inasmuch as ascertainment of sahams among the co-sharers can only be done by a competent civil Court, and the Revenue Officers under the SAT Act, having not the status and power of a Court, cannot order for apportionments of the saham. He, then, places Section 143B of the SAT Act and forcefully submits that a revision in the record-of-rights by distribution of the respective shares of any land to the co-sharers can only be done by fulfilling the requirements outlined therein. In continuation of his submission on this point, he argues that if there are conflicting claims by the co-sharers as to the title and possession of a landed property, the A/C Land cannot proceed with a mutation case until the dispute is settled by a competent Court of law. 

 11. Per contra, Mr. Md. Borhanuddin, the learned Advocate claims that he represents respondent nos. 7-10. At the very outset, he refers to annexure-Z to the affidavit-in-opposition and submits that the basis of the petitioner’s claim is Rent Suit no.1785 of 1950 but from the annexure-Z, it is evident that the said suit was not about the present suit land and, accordingly, he submits that the papers and documents produced in corroboration of the title and possession of the suit land on the basis of the said Rent Suit no. 1785 of 1950 are forged. He, then, refers to annexure-Z1 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent nos. 7-10, which is the SA Khatian no. 233, and submits that the said respondents are the co-sharers with the petitioner’s vendor Md. Abdul Wahab, and since no share was stated in the said SA Khatian, it is to be taken that all the 6 (six) persons named in the SA Khatian are the owners with equal shares and, accordingly, it is the submission of the learned Advocate for respondent nos. 7-10 that while Md. Abdul Wahab was legally owner of only 2.51 acres of land, he was not competent and entitled to sell 10.33 acres of land and to execute and register the sale deed no. 5365 dated 03.06.1985 in favour of the petitioner. Finally, he submits that the civil suit has been instituted by these respondents for partition of the ejmali properties and, on the other hand, the application for review under Section 150 of the SAT Act, which has been registered as Miscellaneous Case no. 2/08-09, was filed by them before the A/C Land for correction of mutation cancelling the petitioner’s Mutation Case no. 380(IX-I)/85-86 and, thus, it is argued that given the nature of the remedy sought for by respondent nos. 7-10 in the civil suit and in the mutation proceedings, the above two moves were required to make in two different fora and, further, in view of the provisions of the SAT Act, barring institution of any suit against the orders passed by the Revenue Officers, these respondents have rightly moved the A/C Land and, thus, there is no wrong in the impugned order. 

 19. It is the submission of the learned Advocate for respondent nos. 7-9 that the functions performed or orders passed by the Revenue Officers are beyond the periphery of the jurisdiction of the civil Courts and, thus, alongside the civil suit, which would determine and adjudicate mainly the saham and title but not be capable of changing the names in the record-of-rights, they had to approach the A/C Land for correction of the record-ofrights. In order to deal with the above submission, we are required to look at the concerned Sections of the SAT Act seeking to oust the jurisdiction of the civil Courts. The following Sections, namely Sections 30, 46B, 69, 72, 86A, 115, 134, 144B and 145F of the SAT Act put an embargo to take recourse to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts. 

 20. From a minute reading of the above provisions, it appears that Section 30 prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when an order is made directing preparation or revision of a record-of-rights, Section 46B puts the said embargo when Compensation Assessment-roll has been prepared. Also, as per Section 69, until all the rent receivers’ interests, which were liable to be acquired, have been acquired, the rent receivers were made ineligible to file any execution case for recovery of their interests, Section 72 prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when Compensation Assessment-roll has been published, Section 86A puts a bar to sue with regard to the right in any land which re-appears on account of alluvion or abatement of rent on account of diluvion, Section 115 ousts the jurisdiction of the civil Courts in respect of the determination of rentrates, Section 134 prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when an order is passed relating to consolidation of holdings of raiyats, Section 144B prohibits resorting to the jurisdiction of the civil Courts when an order has been made under Section 144(1) directing the preparation of revision of the record-of-rights in respect of any area and Section 145F puts an embargo to institute a suit in the civil Court with regard to a matter which is triable by the Land Survey Tribunal. Out of the above Sections, while Sections 30, 46B, 69 and 72 are the relevant provisions for acquisition, the rest Sections are linked up with the provisions of resolving the tenancy issues. 

 22. However, the fact of the instant case does not attract any of the above barring provisions of the SAT Act given that the petitioner’s case is covered by Section 143 of the SAT Act which does not put any bar to seek remedy in the civil Court. In view of the fact that the petitioner is claiming the case property on the basis of a registered sale deed, respondent nos. 7-9 appear to have rightly invoked the civil Court’s jurisdiction where they will have all the opportunity to examine their title & partition vis-a-vis that of their co-sharers on the case land and, then, pursuant to the judgment and decree from the civil Court, the A/C Land shall be duty bound to update the record-of-rights on the case land. It follows that respondent nos. 7-9 were not legally allowed to approach the A/C Land for correction of the record-of-rights at a time, when the same dispute and grievance is being taken care of by a competent civil Court. 

 When Revenue Officer is appointed for the purpose of preparation or revision of a record-of-rights, or for the purpose of preparation of Compensation Assessment Roll under Part IV of the Act, within any district, part of a district or local area, he shall be appointed either with or without the additional designation of ‘Settlement Officer’ or ‘Assistant Settlement Officer’. Every such officer is hereby vested with- 

 36. Power vested in Revenue Officers- When a Revenue-officer is appointed for the purpose of revision of a record-of-rights under chapter XVII of the Act within any district, part of a district or local area, he shall be appointed either with or without the additional designation of “Settlement Officer” or “Assistant Settlement Officer”. Every such Officer shall have,- 

 143. Maintenance of the record-or-rights: The Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-or-rights prepared or revised under Part IV, or under this Part by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 

 32. From a minute reading of the above provisions of law, it appears that the duty of maintenance of the record-of-rights has been conferred upon the Collectors and he, with the assistance of the sub-ordinate Revenue Officers, shall perform the said duty apparently on two occasions. Firstly, when a clerical mistake occurs in passing an order on mutation, or after preparation of the record-of-rights or after revision of the same under Part VI of the SAT Act and, secondly, when there is any change in the ownership of the land as a result of transfer/inheritance, or on account of the events having taken place as enunciated in sub-Sections (b) to (d) of Section 143 of the SAT Act. 

 33. To put the provisions of Section 143(a) in a bit detail, it may be said that under Section 89 of the SAT Act, the happening of any transfer of land, upon being registered by the registering officer, must be notified to the Revenue Officer whose duty, then, becomes to open a file for mutation of record of rights and issue notice to the co-sharers of the transferred land, as provided in Section 143C of the SAT Act. However, if the landed property is acquired by inheritance and the partition taken place amicably through a registered instrument upon observing the provisions of the personal laws, Section 143B(2) of the SAT Act empowers the Revenue Officers to cause changes in the record-of-rights. On the other hand, the provisions of Section 143(b) to (d) of the SAT Act provide that if there is any amalgamation of land under Section 116 of the SAT Act, or subdivision of a joint tenancy under Section 117 of the SAT Act, or there happens a consolidation of holdings under Section 125 of the SAT Act, the Revenue Officer under the authority of the Collector shall incorporate the said changes in the record-of-rights. Also, whenever there is the new settlement of the lands or the Government purchases holdings, or there is abatement of rent on account of abandonment, diluvion and acquisition of land, the Collector’s duty is to cause the said changes in the record-of-rights. 

 34. From the facts of the case at hand, it surfaces that there has been a transfer, as per the claim of the petitioner, by Md. Abdul Wahab Mondal, who is the father of the petitioner as well as of respondent nos. 7-9 and, accordingly, the petitioner had approached the concerned Revenue Officer namely, A/C Land, Debhatta, Stakhira, in the year 1985 by filing an application under Section 117 read with Section 143 of the SAT Act and through opening up the Mutation Case no. 380 (IX-I) 85-86 under the authority of Section 143(C) of the SAT Act, the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira, at first, on 03/10/1985 had asked the Tahshilddar to submit a report thereon after making necessary inquires and on 15.10.1985, upon receiving the said report from the Tahshilddar, the record-of-rights was updated by the said Revenue Officer, Debhatta, Satkhira and, accordingly, in our way of scrutiny, we find that the duty performed by the said Revenue Officer namely, A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira, was completely in conformity with the provisions of Sections 117, 143 and 143C of the SAT Act and Rules 22- 24 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 inasmuch as under Section 143 of the SAT Act together with the provisions of relevant rules, namely rules 22-24 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Collectors, with the aid of the Revenue Officers, have been vested with the duty to maintain the record-of-rights of the lands of this country and they are empowered to correct any clerical mistakes occurred in preparation or revision of the record-of-rights and, also, to amend the same when any change takes place in the ownership of the land, be it for sale, inheritance, vesting the property in the Government, acquisition or purchase by the Government etc. 

 36. However, there is no observation by the said A/C Land as to the pendency of the civil suit. Though both the sides now unequivocally admit that a civil suit is pending before the competent Court of law with regard to the claim on the suit property, however, nothing was mentioned about it before the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira neither by respondent nos. 7-9, nor by the writ petitioner. The reasons and motives of non-mentioning about the pendency of the suit are different for the petitioner and respondent nos. 7-9 and, in fact, opposite to each other. While it appears from the contents of the application, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case no. 02/08-09, made by respondent nos. 7-10 before the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira, which has been placed before this Court as annexure-Y, that respondent nos. 7-9 cunningly remained silent about it, in contrast, the petitioner appears to have felt it not necessary to present this information to the A/C Land. Although the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira rejected the said Miscellaneous Case no. 02/08-09 filed by respondent nos. 7-10, however, had the fact of the pendency of the civil suit been stated in the application by respondent nos. 7-10, the A/C Land would have an occasion to make his observation on this fact as well. When these respondents approached the appellate authority namely, Collector the appeal was allowed in absence of the petitioner and, thus, there was no scope for the petitioner to inform the Collector about the pendency of the civil suit on the same claim. Under the circumstance, the petitioner approached the superior appellate authority namely, Divisional Commissioner, Khulna who affirmed the order of the Collector, Satkhira without discussing the fact of institution of the civil suit. Finally, when the petitioner moved the Land Appeal Board where it transpires that the petitioner stated about the facts of the civil suit but the said final appellate authority did not take up the said issue for its consideration and simply arrived at a decision that the order passed by the Collector, Debhatta, Satkhira, to the effect that the record is required to be upgraded by distributing the share to the co-sharers named in the S.A. Khatian no. 233, does not suffer from any infirmity. As the last and final authority on the mutation matters, the Full Board of Land Appeal Board was expected to be astute in discharging their duties, for, a judicious order passed by the said final authority not only minimises the hassle of the parties to a mutation proceeding, which the litigant experience in dealing with the mutation cases, but it also saves the invaluable time of this Court. 

 38. The above core issue of this case surfaces to be a rare one of its kind in this Court as our research could not trace out any similar case on this point. On the other hand, there is no statutory provision as well to guide us a clear-cut path for adjudication upon the point. Under the circumstances, we have no other option but to put our best effort, based on sound and pertinent reasoning to adjudicate upon the issue. It is a universally recognized rule that Parliament or Executive does not take up any sub-judice matter for their consideration. The principle is rooted in our Constitution as well as in many of statutes of our country, including the Rules of the Procedure of Parliament, and, accordingly, it would be a sound and rational view to hold that if there is a case pending in a competent Court of law regarding any dispute over any land property and on the same dispute, pending disposal of the said case, a Revenue Officer is subsequently approached by any claimant with a prayer to update a record-of-rights in the form of amendment or the correction of the record-of-rights, the Revenue Officer should abstain from proceeding with the mutation case. 

 39. In the case at hand, all the Revenue Officers, from the A/C Land to the Land Appeal Board, utterly failed to address this issue. While it is apparent that the parties to this case were at fault at the initial stage before the A/C Land and the Collector for not disclosing the fact of pendency of the civil suit and, later on, when the petitioner had presented the said fact, although belatedly, the Divisional Commissioner and the Land Appeal Board failed to take up the fact for their consideration. Moreover, unless a Revenue authority is presented with a registered instrument of amicable settlement or the contending parties of a mutation case agrees on their respective shares, no Revenue Authority is competent to change the record-of-rights by apportioning/allocating shares to the claimants of any landed property. Thus, in the instant case, the first appellate authority namely, Collector, Satkhira when passed the order stating that the A/C Land, Debhatta, Satkhira should update the record by distributing the share, we find that the said appellate authority exceeded its jurisdiction having attempted to usurp the functions of a civil Court inasmuch as it is for the civil Court to decide the share of the landed property in a situation where the claimed co-sharers are not in agreement as to their respective shares. 

 40. We are of the view that in dealing with the mutation proceedings the Revenue Officers’ duties are only to record the names of the owners of the land upon examining the relevant papers and documents, if the same are produced before them without raising/taking any objection thereto. But the moment the Revenue Officer would come to know, either through an enquiry conducted by him with the assistance of the Tahshilder or any other staff of his office, or through an application filed by a private party for mutation, that there are disputes regarding the produced papers and documents and there are contending claimants over any land and the matter is pending in the Court for disposal, the concerned Revenue Officer must not proceed further with regard to the said mutation case until the said civil suit is finally disposed of. 

 41. In this case, it is an admitted fact that respondent nos. 7-9 have already invoked the competent jurisdiction, namely the jurisdiction of the civil Court, seeking cancellation of the mutation recorded in favour of the petitioner in the year 1985 together with a prayer for partition of the suit land and, thus, we are of the view that until their respective title is settled by the civil Court, the Revenue Officer shall not be in a position to distribute or apportion the respective portions of the share of the petitioner and that of respondent nos. 7-9 for recording the same in their respective record-of-rights. 

 42. Accordingly, we hold that the order passed by all the appellate authorities, starting from the Collector of Satkhira upto the Land Appeal Board, committed illegality in holding that the record-of-rights should be amended upon allocating the sahams among the contending parties. It follows that the impugned order is destined to be declared illegal and, thereby, the same requires to be set aside. 

 (2) Respondent no. 6, being the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Debhatta, Satkhira, is directed to take his decision on updating the record-of-rights of the parties of Miscellaneous Case no. 47 of 2010 only when the adjudication of the Title Suit no. 50 of 2013, now pending before the Court of learned 2nd Joint District Judge, Satkhira, is finally completed. 

 (3) Respondent no. 1, being the Secretary of the Land Ministry, is directed that he shall, in an endeavour to prevent the recurrence of recording a mutation during pendency of a civil suit, issue a circular notifying all the Revenue Officers of Bangladesh and also the that if a civil suit is pending involving claim of title on the basis of transfer or inheritance of an immovable property, the said Officers and the Board shall not, whether suo-motu or upon an application of any person, entertain a case for mutation of names in the record-of-rights under Section 143(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 till a final decision is arrived at in such civil suit through exhausting appeal or revision arising therefrom.

The appeal was heard by the Second Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, who affirmed the judgment of the Trial Court holding "The learned Trail Court accepted the defendant's contention as of substance and held that the Debuttarnarna Ext.-1 was not acted upon. 1 also find nothing to differ from him. Exhibits A and B conclusively proves the defendant's contention that Ramoni Mohan even after executing Debuttarnama in the year 1351 B.S. in respect of the jama and holding in brought Rent Suit No.182 of 1952 in respect of same jama and holding in his individual capacity giving an absolute go-bye to Ext.]. This shows clearly that this Ext.1 was not acted upon nor was it meant to be acted upon by Ramoni Mohan even during his life time "This contention- of the tenant, defdts was corroborated to the fullest extent by plff. No.2. But 1 may observe here that there is an apparent clash of interest between plff. No.1 and plff. No.2 and for that purpose I would like to leave the question of title of plff. No.1 and 2 interest open for a decision in a properly constituted suit between them as there is no scope for any finding of their title in the present suit or appeal." Referring to exhibit-7, the learned counsel submitted that the Trial Court committed error of law in finding contrary to the recital of the deed in as much as the Trial Court without considering the original deed has drawn conclusion on surmises but in fact Ramoni Mohan executed deed on 11.2.1952 and the schedule of both the deeds indicated that the preliminary number remains the same and in view of such facts the Appellate Court upon discharging the entire evidence held that the deeds were not acted upon and thus committed no error of law. He further contends that from exhibit-"Uma" it would be evident that the last alleged Shebait had come to Sylhet but did not convene meeting but the Hindu locals allegedly held the meeting on 23.5.1972 and in the meeting the alleged committee for the management of the property was formed and for the self same property the plaintiff filed suit before 1972 and the plaintiff was not notified while convened the meeting by the locals which is also evident from the exhibit "Uma" and alleged committee admittedly had formed in the absence of the plaintiff and this vital aspect of the case has not been considered by the Trial Court. The learned Counsel further submitted that from the evidence of the DWs it has been indicated that "idol" / deities had been shifted to house of the Secretary, the alleged Shebait and the Shebait is residing in his personal property and thus public has got no excess there. It would be evident further from the evidence that the alleged deitie's house of Akhara Bari has got no existence, what so ever, in spite of such evidence on record, such basic point, the Trial Court has not at all considered but this vital aspect of the case has been thoroughly considered by the Appellate Court and held that the deities have no existence and consequently, held that the deeds were not acted upon and therefore, committed no error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned counsel further submitted that the plaintiff is not bound by any action of the alleged committee to have taken after the filing of the suit in 1969 and such actions are bad in law and suffers from principle of Lis pendens, as completed under section 52 of the Transfer Property Act and the alleged recording of name of the alleged Shebait after 1969 has got no validity and as such, the plaintiff is not bound by such recording allegedly made in the name of the alleged deities, but such aspect of the case was not considered by the Trial Court. He submitted further that natural corollary is that admittedly the plaintiff is the only heir of Ramoni Mohan and after the death of Ramoni automatically, the title and the possession of the property had vested on the plaintiff, if no contrary title is established by producing any legal evidence and accordingly, the name of the plaintiff was recorded in the S.A. Khatian and paid the rents denying the existence of the deities, 

 16. On perusal of the judgment of the Appellate Court, it transpires that the Appellate Court has reversed the findings and decision of the Trial Court and held that the dedication to have made by 2 documents by Ramoni Mohan had not been acted upon as the donor had not completely divested himself of all beneficial interest in the property given in endowment and that the plaintiff is the legal heir of the said Ramoni Mohan and he has interest in the land and further held perusing the exhibits, in as much as the judgments of the litigations have expressly disclosed that Ramoni Mohan Das during his life time realized rent from the tenants and also for arrear of rents had filed rent suits and his name also was recorded in S.A. Khatian which is evident from exhibit-Gha(1) and further that such recording of rights has not been challenged 

 18. The Appellate Court has held relying upon mainly on the S.A. Khatian exhibit 2-2('), sale deed dated 22/02/1952 exhibit 7 and order dated 5.1.1959 in rent suit no.44 of 1958 and also on the basis of the order passed in Rent appeal No.16 of 1959 (arose out of rent suit no.44 of 1958) that the plaintiff has been able to prove that during the life time of said Ramoni Mohan, he did not divest himself from the properties rather he mutated his name and realized rent. The A"ppellate Court also held that the plaintiff is admittedly the grand son of Ramoni Mohan and the title and possession naturally had vested in him. He also found that the deities were not kept in the Debuttar properties but allegedly preserved in the custody of the Secretary of the committee in his personal house and also found that alleged application made by Ramoni Mohan contained no schedule of the property and as such, recording of names in S.A. Khatian remained unchallenged and I am of the view that the Appellate Court has decided the matter to its true perspective considering the evidence both oral and documentary and law and in reversing the findings, it appears further that the Appellate Court has committed no error of law. I have also concentrated myself as to whether the deeds ' were acted upon and upon scrutiny found that the original maker of the deeds i.e. Ramoni Mohan had recorded his name in S.A. Khatian during his life time and Braja Bala tried to establish herself as the Shebait by filing rent suit but the Munsif, 1st Court, Sylhet in rent suit no.44 of 1958 which had clearly held that the deeds were not acted upon and such findings were affirmed by the Appellate Court with the opinion that in an appropriate constituted suit the fate of the deeds will be decided and accordingly, the plaintiff had filed the suit in 1969. It appears from the resolution of the meeting held on 23.5.1972 Braja Bala was not present. The life of the committee appears to have given by the learned District Judge till appointment of the Shebait and since the plaintiff has been able to prove that the dedication of properties made by Ramoni Mohan by 2 deeds were not acted upon and further held that the function of the committee thereby ceased and in holding as such, the Appellate Court has committed no error of law. It is in evidence that the del'ies are not being maintained in the land of the Debuttar property but kept in a private house of the Secretary and as such, the very purpose of dedication as it appears to have lost and as such, I am of the opinion that the plaintiff has been able to prove that the Endowments had been made were "Illusory endowments and "Illusory endowments" are sham endowments. In such endowment the donor does not completely divest himself of all beneficial interest in the property given in endowment. 

 19. It has been found from the evidence on record that the Secretary of the Committee had removed the temple in which those were installed and installed those in his private house, where the member of the Hindu community appears to have no excess and thus, the worshippers are depriving in giving Sheba-puja. 

 24. The office is directed to send down the lower courts records immediately.

3. Defendant No. I contested the suit by filing written statements and contended inter alia that, the suit was barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties and also stated that, the proforma defendant Nos. 13 and 14 never executed any Bainapatra or delivered possession of the suit land, that Suresh had no son in the name of Sankar (Proforma opposite party No. 14), but died leaving behind two sons namely Subrata and Shuhendu; that Ratish Chowdhury proforma defendant No. 13 sold Dag No. 2569 of the 2nd schedule comprising an area of 2.16 acres to this defendant by, registered kabala dated 03.06.1972 and delivered possession thereof and since then this defendant was possessing the same. The further case of the defendant petitioner was that Subrata and Shubendu sons of Suresh Chowdhury contracted to sell Dag No. 2283 of the 2nd schedule land with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on 10.04.1964 and delivered possession thereof. That the defendant took settlement in 1358 B.S. of the suit 3rd scheduled land from the zamindar Romesh Chandra Chowdhury and Suresh Chandra Chowdhury and since then was possessing the same as residence and living there with their family. That as the record of right wrongly prepared in the name of Ex-land Lord, this defendant filed Title Suit No. 150 of 1969 in the first court of Munsif Sylhet for correction of the record of rights; that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 202 of 19769 was not binding upon this defendant as he was not a party to the suit and that the plaintiff had no right title or interest over the suit land and hence prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 7. Mr. M. A. Samid with, Mr. M.G.H. Ruhullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submitted that both the courts below acted legally and com-mitted no mistake in passing their judgments and decrees. He further argued that the trial court rightly observed that Suresh had only one son which was evident from the fact that the defendant in Title Suit No. 150 of 1969 for correction of record of right made Subrata Chowdhury son of late Suresh Chowdhury as defendant No. 2 and none else and this clearly showed that Suresh had only one son and it also got strength from the certified copy of the petition filed by defendant in Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1970. In the said petition Sunkar was admitted by the defendant as only son of Suresh and from this evidence it was clear that Suresh had only one son namely Sankar and not Subrata. He also submitted that the lower appellate court had rightly observed that Ext.-C হইতেছে দেওয়ানী ১৫০/১৯৬৯ নং মোকদ্দমার ডিক্রীর সই মুহুরী নকল। উক্ত দেওয়ানী ১৫০/১৯৬৯ নং মোকদ্দমাটি বাদী ইন্তাজ আলী দায়ের করেন রেকর্ড সংশোধনের মোকদ্দমা এবং উক্ত মোকদ্দমার ২নং বিবাদী হিসাবে সুব্রত চন্দ্র চৌধুরী পিল মৃত সুরেশ চন্দ্র চৌধুরীকে একমাত্র ছেলে হিসাবে দেখানো হয়েছে। পি.ডব্লিউ-১ অঞ্জন খা তাহার জবান বন্দীতে বলেন ১৪নং বিবাদী শংকর প্রসাদ চৌধুরী সুরেশ চন্দ্র এর একমাত্র ছেলে। --------   and on this score the lower appellate court had observed that though the defendant No. 1, dismissed the decree of the Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 and also Title Execution No. 5 of 1970 but the defendant did not file any suit challenging the legality of Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 and Title execution Case No. 5 of 1970 and as such the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial court in Title Suit No. 202 of 1969 was valid in the eye of law. He finally argued that the petitioner never was in possession of the suit property since he neither mentioned his possession any where in written statement or memo appeal or Revisional application. In support of his argument he referred the cases of Zamir Uddin Ahmed Vs. Ziaul Huq and others, reported in 49 DLR622 and Md. Shah Alam Vs. Musammat Panda Begum, reported in 17BLD(AD)145. 

 8. I have perused the materials on record and it is found that both the courts below elaborately have considered all the aspects of the case. The Courts below categorically discussed the evidence on record of both the sides and other materials in passing their judgments and decrees. I have also observed the referred decisions and the way the courts below made observation on evidence and other materials on record which in my opinion both the courts below committed no error of law. In the situation this case has no merit and nothing to interfere with the judgments and decrees of the courts below. 

 Lower courts record be sent down at once.

fulldatas.lawyer:
Md Rowshan Ali, Advocate -For the Petitioners
Md Nazrul Islam, Advocate -For the Opposite Parties
fulldatas.parties:
Karimon Nessa being dead her heir Chand Ali Pramanik and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Sorab Ali and others ------ Opposite Parties
fulldatas.full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of this Rule are that Karimon Nessa, deceased mother of the present plaintiff petitioners, instituted the above noted original suit for having a declaration of title in the suit land measuring 3.37 acres as described in the schedule "G" to the plaint. According to her case, 'ka' schedule land measuring an area of 5.00 acres including the suit land as recorded under CS Khatian No. 56 previously belonged to 3 sisters namely; Golejan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi in equal shares. Rupejan Bibi died leaving her heirs in 2 sisters. Thereafter, Golejan Bibi died leaving her husband Saimuddin and sister Sukjan Bibi, Subsequently, Sukjan Bibi died leaving the plaintiff Karimon Nessa as daughter, who also got the share of Saimuddin by purchase. That the plaintiff and Golejan Bibi previously transferred 0.87 acres of land to Ayet Ali who has also possession therein. SA Khatian in respect of the said transferred land along with the some other lands were prepared accordingly in the name of the plaintiff and Ayet Ali, which is shown in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint. That when the plaintiff was the actual owner and possessor of the remaining 'Ga' schedule land (suit land) it was once sold in auction on 21-11-1953 in Rent Execution Case No. 770 of 1953 and ex-landlord was shown to have purchased the land paper, but possession was never delivered to him after the said auction sale. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1959, in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Pabna for setting aside the auction sale under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Accordingly, the disputed auction sale was set aside in the proceeding by the learned Munsif vide an order dated 23-5-1959. Therefore, the suit land remained under the ownership of the plaintiff as it was before. But subsequently, during SA operation, the suit land was wrongly recorded as khas land of the Government (defendant No. 1) on the basis of said wrong SA Khatian. Two lease cases were collusively started in the years 1970-71 and lease order was issued in favour of the defendant No. 2 Sobhan Ali Sheikh. On being aware of the aforesaid, settlement to the defendant No. 2 on 10-4-1975, the plaintiff filed the present suit for having a declaration of her title in the suit property. The defendant No. 1, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, did not contest the suit. The defendant No. 2 Md Sorab Ali Sheikh contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the 'Ka' Schedule land originally belonged to Kachir Mondal who died leaving 3 daughters namely, Golejan Bibi, Rupjan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi, one wife Moyful and 3 cousins (paternal) namely; Biru, Hiru and Miru. Rapjan Bibi died leaving her husband Gumani Mridha, mother Moyful and 2 sisters Golejan and Sukjan. Thereafter Sukjan Bibi died leaving her husband Pabna, mother Moyful, sister Golejan Bibi and daughter (plaintiff). Then Moyful died leaving her daughter Golejan Bibi, second husband Bina Mondal and daughter Elajan. Thereafter, Golejan Bibi died leaving her husband Saimuddin and Cousin Subid Mondal Miru Mondal was survived by his only son Subid Mondal. Hiru Mondal died unmarried leaving his brother Biru Mondal, Elajan, daughter of Biru Mondal, died leaving her father and 2 daughters in Sakina and Bashabi Bewa. Biru Mondal left his second wife Tolajan and nephew Mondal as heirs. Thereafter Subid Mondal, Tolajan Bibi and Pabna (husband of Sukja) sold 2.97 acres of land by 2 registered Kabalas dated 2-4-1968 and 12-4-1968. Subsequently, when the defendant No. 2 found that the suit land was sold in auction sale and the Government acquired ownership, he took lease from the Government vide Settlement Case No. 9 of 1970-71 and 14 of 1970-71 and continued possession in the suit property. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 410 of 1968 against the Government for correction of record, which was dismissed. So, the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned Subordinate Judge, on hearing both the sides and considering evidence adduced by the parties decreed the suit on contest on 30-4-1987 declaring plaintiffs title to the suit land. Against the said Judgment and decree the contesting defendant No. 2 filed an appeal, which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Pabna. The appellate Court on hearing both the sides allowed the appeal of the defendant No. 2 and reversed the judgment passed by the trial Court and consequently the original suit stood dismissed by his judgment dated 14-3-1996. 

 4. The learned Senior Advocate Mr Rowshan Ali, appearing on behalf of the petitioner (plaintiff), has taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and the evidence on record. He submits that since the issue Nos. 2-3 relating to maintainability and limitation of the suit were not agitated before the trial Court, the appellate Court wrongly reopened the matters out of the way and took wrong decisions in respect of those issues uncalled for. It is submitted that the claim of the plaintiff is based on CS Khatian, which has got presumptive value as to its correctness but the learned Additional District Judge, discarded the said document at the instance of fictitious story introduced by the defendant No. 2 after a long span of time. That the defendant No. 2 never challenged the CS Khatian at any point of time in assertion of their interest. He submits that the defendant No. 2 also brought two conflicting stories of acquiring interest in the suit land, one from the alleged purchase from some fictitious co-sharers in the year 1968 and another by way of taking settlement from the Government admitting that he had no independent title in the land. It is further submitted that when the collusive auction sale was set aside, the ex-landlord or the successor Government did not acquire any interest in the said auction sale to hold its management and give settlement of the plaintiff's suit land. He has made further submission supporting the findings and decisions arrived at by the trial Court. It is submitted that the plaintiff petitioners, being the heirs of the original admitted owners, are in physical possession having title therein and they will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court are not set aside. 

 5. The learned Senior Advocate Mr Nazrul Islam, appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, submits that the findings and decision arrived at by the learned appellate Court are based on reasons and supported by the evidence on record. It is submitted that the plaintiffs were aware of the alleged wrong SA Khatian prepared in the name of the Government when a suit was filed by the plaintiff for correction of record under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the year 1968. So, the present suit having been filed after 6 years from the said knowledge of wrong record, was barred under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. It is further submitted that the cause of action of this suit, has not been proved. According to his submission, the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court are based on evidence on record and there being instance of misreading and non-consideration of evidence, the said judgment does not call for interference. 

 6. Admittedly, the suit land measuring 3.37 acres of land (Ga-Schedule including some other lands were recorded in the names of 3 sisters namely, Golejan Bibi, Rupjan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi in equal shares during Cadastral Survey (CS Operation). Exhibit 5 CC Khatian No. 56 stands in support of the contentions as to the previous ownership of the suit land according to the plaintiff's case, Sale Certificate dated 12-1-1954 (Boinama) submitted by the defendant in connection with Rent Execution Case No. 720 of 1953 filed by the ex-landlord Raja Protiva Nath Roy Bahadur against the original plaintiff Karimon Nessa and another CS recorded owner Golejan Bibi (her Khala). It indicates clearly that said plaintiff Karimon Nessa was the owner of the suit land with Golejan Bibi in the year 1953-54 when the auction sale was held. None of the defendant No. 2's predecessors, according to his genealogy given in the written statement, was party to the execution proceedings of the connected Rent suit which he relied on. Had they any interest and possession in the suit land according to the defendant's case, their names ought to have appeared amongst the defaulter tenants against whom auction proceeding was initiated. The defendant No. 2 though set up a separate case stating genealogy of Kichir Mondal, father of the CS recorded tenants as previous owner, he has not been able to establish such contention by substantial evidence in view of consistency in the plaintiffs clear case on the basis of CS Khatian. So, the defendant's case so far his claim of independent ownership through reversion heirs of Kichir Mondal, cannot be acceptable. Further, it is evident that actually the case of the defendant stands on the second contention ie termination of plaintiffs tenancy right, in the suit land on the basis of auction purchase by the ex-landlord Raja Protiva Nath Roy Bahadur. The defendant No. 2 relying on the auction sale submitted Bainanama dated 12-4-1954, which is Exhibit I. After the promulgation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the suit land, alleged to have been auction purchased by the ex-landlord, vested in the Government as non-retainable Khas land. So, the defendant No. 2 prayed that the suit land was correctly recorded in the name of the Government during SA operation giving a complete go-by to his earlier stand of independent claim of title. Accordingly, the defendant No. 2 took lease from the Government vide Exhibit 3 which shows that the lease was given showing the suit land as khas land of the Government in the year 1974. In such view of the matter, it must be held that the CS Khatian can be taken as the basis of asserting ownership of the suit land and the plaintiff Karimon Nessa was admitted to be owner of the suit land as she was shown as judgment debtor of the Execution Case through which the admitted auction sale took place on 21-11-1953. 

 7. Thus, it appears that if the auction sale on the basis of Exhibit 1 stands good, then the defendant No. 2 has a defendable case of claiming possessor right on the basis of lease deed executed by the Government treating the suit land as non-retainable khas case land of the ex-landlord. In other words, if the SA Khatian is found to be correct, then only the defendant No. 2 is entitled to effectively resist the claim of the plaintiff as a leaseholder under the Government, otherwise not. Exhibit 3 is the Certified Copy of a petition filed by the plaintiff on 2-2-1959 under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1849 for setting aside the auction sale, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1959 against the decree holder ex-landlord who was replaced by the Government, alleging that the auction was held in a fraudulent manner by suppressing notice on the plaintiff who was in physical possession. It appears that from Exhibit 4 that the said Miscellaneous Case was allowed setting aside the auction sale by the learned Munsif on 23-5-1959 and the plaintiff also paid arrears rent to the Government vide challan dated 17-4-1959 which is marked as Exhibit 2. In view of the order setting aside the prior auction sale in respect of the suit land, the plaintiffs title and possession cannot be said to have been terminated. Had she not been in physical possession, the application for setting aside the auction sale need not have been brought by her in the year 1959. It may be mentioned here that the decree holder auction purchaser did not take delivery of possession in the suit land in pursuance of the said auction sale, which had been subsequently set aside by the competent Court. No writ of delivery of possession is available. So, there is no reason to record the disputed land in the name of the Government as Khas land during SA Operation which was done after setting aside the auction sale in the year 1959. It is therefore, apparently a wrong record of right and the said Khatian in respect of the suit land ought to have been recorded in the name of original plaintiff Most. Karimon Nessa. So, the petitioners being admitted heirs of Karimon Nessa appear to have acquired good title in the suit land by way of inheritance. So far possession in the suit land is concerned, the plaintiff's side produced some Government dakhilas (Exhibit 1 series) and adduced 5 witnesses. They also paid arrear rent by a challan (Exhibit 2). All the PWs gave testimony in support of the plaintiffs possession, whereas 4 DWs said about possession of both the parties in the suit land. So, the assertion of plaintiffs possession gets affirmation by many DWs at least in respect of some portion of the suit land. The learned trial Court appears to have elaborately discussed evidence of possession and arrived at a proper finding in support of the plaintiff's possession. The appellate Court appears to have taken erroneous view in the matter of ascertaining possession due to misreading and non-consideration of material evidence on record, which I have already discussed above. 

 8. Mere knowledge about wrong recording of SA Khatian does not give rise to the cause of action to bring any suit, if the plaintiff does not bring such cause of action in the plaint. Limitation shall start running from the date of given cause of action. The learned Additional District Judge, Pabna, appears to have taken a wrong view in holding that since the plaintiff knew about the alleged wrong SA Khatian at the time of filing the suit bearing No. 410 of 1968 the present suit filed in the year 1975 was barred by limitation. He did not see that the plaintiffs cause of action in the present suit arose on 10-4-1975, when she came to know about the lease granted in favour of the defendant No. 2 by the Government. It appears from the lease deed that it was executed and registered on 16-7-1974. So, the plaintiff appears to have filed the suit in time from given cause of action and, as such, the suit cannot be said to have been barred by limitation under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. I have carefully gone through the judgment passed by the appellate Court along with the evidence on record and it is evident that the learned Additional District Judge has failed in error in taking decision in the appeal reversing the findings of the trial Court on the main question of acquisition of title and possession in the suit land. When some of the PWs admitted possession of the plaintiffs in some portion of the suit land, the learned Additional District Judge was totally wrong to find that the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Moreover, the findings arrived at by the learned trial Court on the question of possession appears to be sound and proper. Therefore, I hold the view that the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court were not liable to be set aside in the appeal. 

 9. After the reconsideration of all the materials, facts, circumstances and evidence on record, I am inclined to hold that the appellate Court has fallen in error of law due to the misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record and, as such, it resulted in an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and decree cannot legally be sustained. 

 Send down the lower Court records at once.

Abdul Quayum with AKM Zahirul Huq, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner
Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
